title: Triage Session Widget
text:
The Triage Session Widget provides a structured workflow for reviewing and curating data across video frames. It implements a Mark / Commit / Recall pattern: you mark a starting frame, scrub through the video to review a region, then either commit (execute a batch operation on that region) or recall (abort and return to the mark point).
This widget is especially useful for:

Line triage — reviewing deep-learning predictions and moving correct outputs to a ground-truth dataset.
Interval labeling — inspecting scattered regions of a video and recording which frames have been reviewed.
Multi-step workflows — chaining several operations (move data, record intervals, run transforms) into a single atomic commit.

The Triage Session Widget is accessed via the menu: View → Tools → Triage Session.

title: Triage Session Widget
text:
Widget Layout
The widget is divided into four sections:

Status
Displays the current state of the triage session:

Idle — No marking in progress. Shows the current frame number.
Marking (from X) — Marking is active from frame X. Shows the current frame number.



Controls
Three buttons control the triage workflow:








Button
Enabled When
Action




Mark
Idle
Begin a triage range at the current frame


Commit
Marking (with valid pipeline)
Execute the pipeline for [mark_frame, current_frame]


Recall
Marking
Abort marking and return to Idle without executing anything





Pipeline
The pipeline section defines what happens when you press Commit. A pipeline is a sequence of commands that operate on your data. You can configure the pipeline in two ways:

Load JSON — Load a pre-written pipeline from a .json file.
Guided Editor — Visually build a pipeline by adding commands from a dropdown and filling in parameters with form widgets.

A collapsible Raw JSON section shows the underlying JSON representation and can be edited directly.
See Pipeline Configuration below for details.


Tracked Regions
Shows the number of intervals and total frame count in the tracked-regions DigitalIntervalSeries. This lets you see at a glance how much of the video has been triaged.

title: Triage Session Widget
text:
The Mark / Commit / Recall Workflow
┌───────┐   Mark    ┌─────────┐   Commit   ┌───────┐
│ Idle  │ ────────► │ Marking │ ──────────► │ Idle  │
└───────┘           └─────────┘             └───────┘
                         │
                         │ Recall
                         ▼
                    ┌───────┐
                    │ Idle  │
                    └───────┘

Navigate to the start of a region you want to process.
Press Mark. The widget records the current frame as mark_frame and transitions to the Marking state.
Scrub through the video to the end of the region you want to process.
Press Commit. The pipeline executes with two runtime variables automatically set:

${mark_frame} — the frame where you pressed Mark.
${current_frame} — the frame where you pressed Commit.

The widget returns to Idle. The tracked-regions counter updates to reflect the committed range.

If you change your mind, press Recall to abort and return to Idle without executing anything.

title: Triage Session Widget
text:
Pipeline Configuration
A pipeline is a CommandSequenceDescriptor — a JSON document listing commands to execute in order. Each command has a command_name and a parameters object.

Available Commands







Command
Description




MoveByTimeRange
Move entities in a frame range from one data object to another


CopyByTimeRange
Copy entities in a frame range (source unmodified)


AddInterval
Add an interval to a DigitalIntervalSeries


ForEachKey
Iterate a list and execute sub-commands for each item





Variable Substitution
Parameters can reference variables using the ${variable} syntax:

Runtime variables — ${mark_frame} and ${current_frame} are automatically populated by the triage session when you commit.
Template variables — Define your own in the variables section of the pipeline JSON. These are substituted before execution.



Example Pipeline JSON
{
  "name": "Line Triage Pipeline",
  "version": "1.0",
  "commands": [
    {
      "command_name": "MoveByTimeRange",
      "description": "Move correct predictions to ground truth",
      "parameters": {
        "source_key": "predicted_whisker",
        "destination_key": "ground_truth_whisker",
        "start_frame": "${mark_frame}",
        "end_frame": "${current_frame}"
      }
    },
    {
      "command_name": "AddInterval",
      "description": "Record triaged region",
      "parameters": {
        "interval_key": "tracked_regions",
        "start_frame": "${mark_frame}",
        "end_frame": "${current_frame}",
        "create_if_missing": true
      }
    }
  ]
}


Using the Guided Editor
Instead of writing JSON by hand, you can build a pipeline visually:

Click Add Command… to open the command picker.
Select a command from the list (e.g., MoveByTimeRange).
Fill in the parameter form — text fields for data keys, number fields for frame indices. You can type ${mark_frame} or ${current_frame} in text fields to use runtime variables.
Repeat to add more commands.
Use the arrow buttons to reorder commands, or the × button to remove one.

The guided editor and raw JSON stay synchronized — edits in one are reflected in the other.

title: Point Data
text:
The Points widget appears when Points are enabled in the Feature Tree. It’s designed for viewing, styling, adding, and editing keypoints visible in the Media Viewer.
If you haven’t loaded a keypoint dataset, you can still add keypoints; these changes will be tracked in the Data Manager (see Data Manager → points [link user-ref here]).






Note



Saving and Export: Any additions or edits to keypoints are recorded by the Data Manager and can be exported later as part of your dataset.







RGB (0–255): Enter the Red, Green, and Blue channels to set the keypoint color.

Hex Color: Optionally specify a color using a hex code (e.g., #FF6600).

Color Preview: Shows the current color selection.

Alpha: Controls opacity/transparency of the keypoint in the Media Viewer (higher = more opaque).





Point Size: Sets how large the keypoint appears in the Media Viewer.






Note



Data size vs. display size: The stored keypoint in the Data Manager is always one pixel (a single coordinate). Point Size/Shape only affects on-screen display, not the underlying saved data.


Marker Shape: Choose how the keypoint is drawn in the display:

circle, square, triangle, cross, x, diamond







In the Points widget, find Mouse Mode (dropdown).
Select Select Point.
Click anywhere in the Media Viewer to add a keypoint at that location.
To modify a keypoint, use the same mode to select it and then adjust its location in the media window.






Note



Deleting Keypoints: To delete accidentally added or misplaced keypoints, open the data manager and find the frame that contains the keypoint and delete it (see Data Manager → points [link user-ref here]).







Keep Alpha low to ensure that imagery remains visible under points.

When working with multiple keypoints, use distinct shapes or colors to differentiate labels, annotators, or classes.

title: Naive Bayes Classifier
text: Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier based on Bayes’ theorem with an independence assumption between features. Despite this simplifying assumption, it often performs well in practice, trains very quickly, and produces well-calibrated probability estimates.

title: Naive Bayes Classifier
text: Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier based on Bayes’ theorem with an independence assumption between features. Despite this simplifying assumption, it often performs well in practice, trains very quickly, and produces well-calibrated probability estimates.

title: Naive Bayes Classifier
text:
Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




Epsilon
1e-9
Variance smoothing — added to feature variances to prevent division by zero

title: Naive Bayes Classifier
text:
When to Use

You need fast training (near-instant, even with many features)
Your features are roughly independent of each other
You want probability estimates for each class
You have a multi-class problem with many classes

title: Naive Bayes Classifier
text:
Probability Output
Naive Bayes produces probability estimates derived directly from Bayes’ theorem. The probabilities across all classes sum to 1.0 for each frame.

title: Naive Bayes Classifier
text:
Tips

Naive Bayes works best when features are not strongly correlated
If accuracy is poor, consider whether features are redundant (correlated) — try reducing to independent features
The epsilon parameter rarely needs adjustment unless you have features with extremely low variance

title: Logistic Regression
text: Logistic Regression is a linear classifier that models the probability of class membership using the logistic (sigmoid) function. It is well-suited for binary classification tasks and produces naturally calibrated probability outputs.

title: Logistic Regression
text: Logistic Regression is a linear classifier that models the probability of class membership using the logistic (sigmoid) function. It is well-suited for binary classification tasks and produces naturally calibrated probability outputs.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




Lambda
0.0
L2 regularization strength. Higher values penalize large weights and reduce overfitting.


Step Size
0.01
Optimizer step size for gradient descent


Max Iterations
10000
Maximum number of optimizer iterations (0 = unlimited)

title: Logistic Regression
text:
When to Use

You have a binary classification problem (two classes)
You want well-calibrated probability outputs
Your decision boundary is approximately linear in feature space
You need a simple, interpretable model

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Limitations
Logistic Regression supports binary classification only. For multi-class problems, use Random Forest or Naive Bayes.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Probability Output
Logistic Regression produces probability estimates via the sigmoid function, which are naturally calibrated — a predicted probability of 0.7 means roughly 70% of such frames truly belong to the positive class.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Tips

If the model underfits, decrease lambda (less regularization)
If the model overfits, increase lambda (more regularization)
The threshold for classification can be adjusted in the Prediction panel (default 0.5)

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is a sequence-aware classifier that uses temporal continuity to improve predictions. Unlike frame-based classifiers (Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression) that classify each frame independently, the HMM considers what state the system was in at the previous frame when predicting the current frame.
This makes HMMs ideal for detecting behavioral states that persist over time — for example, periods of whisker contact vs. non-contact, where transitions between states are rare relative to the frame rate.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is a sequence-aware classifier that uses temporal continuity to improve predictions. Unlike frame-based classifiers (Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression) that classify each frame independently, the HMM considers what state the system was in at the previous frame when predicting the current frame.
This makes HMMs ideal for detecting behavioral states that persist over time — for example, periods of whisker contact vs. non-contact, where transitions between states are rare relative to the frame rate.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
How It Works
The HMM assumes your data is generated by a system that:

Has a fixed number of hidden states (e.g., “Contact” and “No Contact”)
Transitions between states according to learned probabilities (e.g., 95% chance of staying in the same state)
Emits observable features (e.g., curvature, distance) drawn from a Gaussian distribution specific to each state

Training learns these transition probabilities and per-state Gaussian distributions from labeled data. Prediction then finds the most likely sequence of hidden states given new observations.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




Number of States
2
Number of hidden states. Use 2 for binary classification tasks.


Tolerance
1e-5
Convergence tolerance for parameter estimation


Diagonal Covariance
Off
Use diagonal covariance matrices for emissions (see below)




Diagonal Covariance
By default the HMM fits a full covariance matrix for each state’s Gaussian emission distribution. When diagonal covariance is enabled (checkbox in Model Configuration), each state stores only a variance per feature instead of a full covariance matrix. This:

Reduces parameters dramatically — from \(M(M+1)/2\) to \(M\) per state (where \(M\) is the number of features)
Improves numerical stability when training data is limited relative to the number of features
Assumes conditional independence of features given the hidden state

Enable this option when you have many features relative to your training data, or if training with full covariance fails or produces unstable results.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
When to Use

Your classification target is a temporal state that persists across consecutive frames
Frame-based classifiers produce “noisy” predictions with many rapid state switches
You have labeled event data (DigitalEventSeries) marking state occurrences
You want smoother predictions that respect temporal coherence

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Label Sources
The HMM supports all label sources available in the ML Workflow widget. The most natural pairing is From Events, which converts point events to binary state labels:







Label Source
How It Works




From Events (recommended for HMM)
Frames with a matching event → state 1; all others → state 0


From Intervals
Frames inside the interval → positive class; outside → negative class


From Groups
Each entity group maps to a class label


From Data Entity Groups
Like Groups, but scoped to a specific data key



To use event-based labels, select the “From Events” radio button in the Label Configuration panel and choose a DigitalEventSeries from the dropdown.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Sequence Segmentation
The HMM automatically detects temporal gaps in your feature data and splits it into contiguous sequences. For example, if your feature tensor covers frames 100–200 and 500–600, the HMM treats these as two separate sequences rather than assuming a continuous transition from frame 200 to frame 500.
Sequences shorter than 2 frames are discarded (a single frame carries no temporal information for an HMM).

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Output
The HMM produces the same outputs as other classifiers:








Output
Type
Description




State intervals
DigitalIntervalSeries
One series per state (e.g., "HMM:Contact", "HMM:NoContact")


State probabilities
AnalogTimeSeries
Per-frame probability of each state (if enabled)


Transition matrix
Displayed in Results panel
Learned state-to-state transition probabilities




Transition Matrix
After training, the Results panel shows the learned transition matrix. For a 2-state model:
         → State 0    → State 1
State 0:   0.97          0.03
State 1:   0.05          0.95
This means: if the system is in State 0, there is a 97% chance it stays in State 0 at the next frame, and a 3% chance it transitions to State 1. High diagonal values indicate states that persist over many frames.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Tips

Start with 2 states for binary classification. Only increase the state count if you know your data has more distinct behavioral modes.
The HMM works best when states are temporally persistent — if your target state changes every few frames, a frame-based classifier may perform equally well.
Z-score normalization is recommended, as Gaussian emissions are sensitive to feature scaling.
If training fails, ensure your training data contains examples of all states and includes at least a few state transitions.
Compare HMM predictions against Random Forest to see if temporal smoothing improves your results.
Enable diagonal covariance if you have many features but limited training data.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Prediction Regions
By default, the HMM predicts on all feature rows. You can restrict predictions to a specific frame range by selecting a DigitalIntervalSeries in the Prediction panel. When a prediction region is selected:

The HMM still runs on the full temporal range covering both your training labels and the prediction region (so it retains temporal context at boundaries)
Output is filtered to only write results for the frames you selected

This is useful when you’ve labeled parts of your recording and want to predict just the unlabeled gap, while still benefiting from the HMM’s awareness of the labeled regions on either side.

Constrained Decoding (Warm-Start)
When a prediction region is adjacent to labeled training data, the HMM can warm-start predictions using the known state at the boundary. For example, if your training labels end at frame 1000 with state “Contact”, the HMM starts predicting frame 1001 from that known state rather than guessing.
This is controlled by the “Constrained decoding” checkbox in the Prediction panel (visible only when using HMM). It is enabled by default and generally improves prediction accuracy at region boundaries.
Constrained decoding has no effect on frame-independent classifiers (Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression).

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Comparison with Frame-Based Classifiers








Aspect
Frame-Based (e.g., Random Forest)
HMM




Temporal context
None — each frame classified independently
Considers previous state via transition probabilities


Prediction smoothness
May produce rapid state switches
Naturally produces smooth state sequences


Training data
Shuffled, order does not matter
Order matters — sequences must be temporally contiguous


Speed
Fast (independent per frame)
Moderate (Viterbi decoding, Forward-Backward)


Best for
Features that are strongly discriminative on their own
States that persist over time with noisy features

title: DBSCAN Clustering
text: DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) discovers clusters of arbitrary shape based on point density. Unlike K-Means, it does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance and can identify noise points that don’t belong to any cluster.

title: DBSCAN Clustering
text: DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) discovers clusters of arbitrary shape based on point density. Unlike K-Means, it does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance and can identify noise points that don’t belong to any cluster.

title: DBSCAN Clustering
text:
Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




Epsilon
1.0
Neighborhood radius — the maximum distance between two points to be considered neighbors


Min Points
5
Minimum number of points required to form a dense region (core point threshold)

title: DBSCAN Clustering
text:
When to Use

You don’t know the number of clusters
Clusters have arbitrary shapes (non-spherical)
Your data contains noise or outliers that should not be assigned to any cluster
Cluster densities are roughly uniform

title: DBSCAN Clustering
text:
Noise Detection
DBSCAN labels points that are not within epsilon distance of at least min_points other points as noise. These points are not assigned to any cluster. The cluster output panel shows the noise point count.

title: DBSCAN Clustering
text:
Output
DBSCAN produces hard cluster assignments plus noise detection:

Entity groups: One putative group per discovered cluster
Interval series: Contiguous runs of each cluster assignment
Noise points: Reported separately, not assigned to any group

title: DBSCAN Clustering
text:
Tips

Epsilon is the most important parameter. If all points are noise, increase epsilon. If everything is one cluster, decrease it.
Enable z-score normalization so that epsilon has consistent meaning across features with different scales
Min Points controls sensitivity: higher values create fewer, larger clusters
Start with min_points = 2 × num_features as a rule of thumb

title: Post-Encoder Feature Extraction
text:
After a deep learning encoder processes each video frame into a feature map [B, C, H, W], a post-encoder module optionally collapses or focuses the spatial dimensions before the result is written to DataManager. This is useful for:

Extracting a single compact feature vector per frame (Global Average Pooling)
Watching features at a tracked anatomical landmark (Spatial Point Extraction)

title: Post-Encoder Feature Extraction
text:
After a deep learning encoder processes each video frame into a feature map [B, C, H, W], a post-encoder module optionally collapses or focuses the spatial dimensions before the result is written to DataManager. This is useful for:

Extracting a single compact feature vector per frame (Global Average Pooling)
Watching features at a tracked anatomical landmark (Spatial Point Extraction)

title: Post-Encoder Feature Extraction
text:
Selecting a Post-Encoder Module
The Post-Encoder Module section appears at the bottom of the Deep Learning widget’s Dynamic Slots panel, below the Outputs section.
Use the Module combo to choose one of:







Option
What it does




None
Passes the encoder output directly to the decoder (default).


Global Average Pooling
Averages across all spatial pixels → [B, C] feature vector per batch.


Spatial Point Extraction
Reads features at a user-tracked 2-D point → [B, C] feature vector per frame.

title: Post-Encoder Feature Extraction
text:
Global Average Pooling

Set Module to Global Average Pooling.
Set the output decoder to TensorToFeatureVector (or a compatible target key).
Run batch inference. A TensorData matrix is written to DataManager when the batch completes. Rows correspond to frames; columns correspond to encoder channels.

title: Post-Encoder Feature Extraction
text:
Spatial Point Extraction

Ensure you have a PointData object loaded that tracks the anatomical location of interest frame by frame (e.g. a whisker base, eye corner).
Set Module to Spatial Point Extraction.
Choose Interpolation: Bilinear (recommended for sub-pixel accuracy) or Nearest (faster).
Select the Point Key from the combo — this should be the PointData key containing the per-frame 2-D coordinates.
Run inference. Before each frame the widget reads the first point from the chosen PointData at that frame index and passes it to the module.

title: Post-Encoder Feature Extraction
text:
Output: TensorData
When TensorToFeatureVector is used as the decoder, results are accumulated across all batch frames and written as a single TensorData object. Each row is one frame and each column is one feature channel. The object can be viewed with the Tensor Inspector or used as input to ML pipelines.






Note



For single-frame inference (Run Frame / Current), a 1-row TensorData is written immediately to DataManager after inference completes.

title: Deep Learning Widget
text:
The Deep Learning widget allows you to run neural network inference on your data directly within Neuralyzer. You can load pre-trained PyTorch models, configure which data sources feed into the model, and write the results back to the DataManager for further analysis.
The widget supports models that transform images, points, masks, and lines — the same data types used throughout Neuralyzer.

title: Deep Learning Widget
text:
The Deep Learning widget allows you to run neural network inference on your data directly within Neuralyzer. You can load pre-trained PyTorch models, configure which data sources feed into the model, and write the results back to the DataManager for further analysis.
The widget supports models that transform images, points, masks, and lines — the same data types used throughout Neuralyzer.

title: Deep Learning Widget
text:
Opening the Widget
Open the Deep Learning widget from the menu:
View → Analysis → Deep Learning
This opens two panels:

Properties panel (right side) — where you configure the model and run inference
View panel (center) — displays model status and inference results

title: Deep Learning Widget
text:
Workflow

1. Select a Model
At the top of the Properties panel, use the Model dropdown to select from available models. Each model describes what inputs it expects and what outputs it produces. A description appears below the dropdown when a model is selected.
Available models are either compiled into Neuralyzer (like NeuroSAM) or loaded from JSON specification files at runtime.


2. Load Weights
In the Weights section:

Click Browse… to locate your model weights file
Supported formats:

.pt2 (AOT Inductor) — recommended, best performance
.pt (TorchScript) — legacy support

The Status indicator shows the current state:

Gray: No model selected
Orange: No weights specified, or file exists but not yet loaded
Red: File not found or loading error
Green: Weights loaded successfully, ready for inference




3. Configure Inputs
Once a model is selected, the Properties panel dynamically generates input configuration sections based on the model’s requirements.

Dynamic Inputs
Dynamic inputs change every frame during inference. For each dynamic input slot:

Source — select a data source from the DataManager dropdown. The dropdown is filtered by compatible data types (e.g., an image input only shows MediaData sources)
Encoder — how to convert the data into a tensor. Pre-selected based on the model’s recommendation, but you can override:

ImageEncoder — for video frames and images
Point2DEncoder — for point/keypoint data
Mask2DEncoder — for binary masks
Line2DEncoder — for polyline/curve data

Mode — encoding strategy (depends on encoder):

Raw — direct pixel values (images)
Binary — 1.0 at data locations, 0.0 elsewhere
Heatmap — Gaussian blob at each data location

Sigma — Gaussian width for Heatmap mode (higher = wider blobs)



Memory Inputs (Static)
Some models use memory/reference frames that are set once and reused across inference. These appear in a separate Memory Inputs section:

Source — select the data source for this memory slot
Time Offset — which frame relative to the current frame to use. For example:

t-1 = one frame before the current frame
t-5 = five frames before the current frame
t0 = the current frame




Boolean Mask Inputs
For models that track which memory slots are active (like NeuroSAM), boolean mask inputs appear as checkboxes. These are automatically managed:

When a memory slot has a data source bound, its checkbox is locked to checked
Slots without data can be manually toggled




4. Configure Outputs
For each model output:

Target — select a DataManager key where results will be written. If the key doesn’t exist yet, it will be created automatically.
Decoder — how to interpret the output tensor:

TensorToMask2D — threshold the output to produce a binary mask
TensorToPoint2D — find the peak activation to produce a point coordinate
TensorToLine2D — threshold, skeletonize, and trace to produce a polyline

Threshold — the cutoff value for mask/line decoding (0.0–1.0). Pixels above this value are included in the output.



5. Run Inference
The bottom of the Properties panel has three controls:

Frame — specify which frame number to process
Batch Size — how many frames to process at once (auto-set from the model’s preference)
Run Frame — run inference on the specified frame number
Current — run inference on the current timeline position (tracks the global timeline)
Run Batch — (coming soon) process multiple consecutive frames

After running, the status updates to show “Inference complete (frame N)” and the decoded results are written to the target DataManager keys.

title: Deep Learning Widget
text:
Example: Running NeuroSAM
NeuroSAM is a segment-anything model for neural data. It uses memory frames to guide segmentation:

Select model: Choose “NeuroSAM” from the dropdown
Load weights: Browse to your NeuroSAM .pt2 or .pt file
Configure inputs:

encoder_image → bind to your video data source
memory_images → bind reference frames with time offsets (e.g., t-1, t-5)
memory_masks → bind reference masks corresponding to the memory frames

Configure output:

probability_map → set a target key (e.g., masks/neurosam_output)
Decoder: TensorToMask2D, Threshold: 0.5

Run: Click Run Frame or Current

The predicted mask appears in the DataManager and can be viewed in the Media Widget.

title: Deep Learning Widget
text:
Tips

Encoder selection matters: Using Heatmap mode with Point2DEncoder produces smoother gradients that many models prefer over Binary mode. Experiment with both.
Threshold tuning: Start with 0.5 for mask outputs and adjust based on your model’s confidence calibration. Lower thresholds capture more area, higher thresholds are more selective.
Memory frames: For models with memory inputs, providing more reference frames with accurate masks generally improves prediction quality.
Device: If CUDA is available, inference automatically runs on GPU. Check the application console output to confirm.

title: Deep Learning Widget
text:
Supported Model Formats









Format
Extension
Description
Recommendation




AOT Inductor
.pt2
Ahead-of-time compiled native kernels
Recommended — best performance


TorchScript
.pt
JIT-traced or scripted model
Legacy support — simplest to export



The backend is automatically detected from the file extension. No manual configuration needed.

title: Transform Widget
text: The Transform Widget is a powerful tool for processing data using the TransformsV2 library. It allows you to build a sequence of operations (a pipeline) to manipulate your data, convert types, and extract features.

title: Transform Widget
text:
Overview
The widget provides a visual interface to:

Select Input Data: Choose the data you want to transform.
Define a Pipeline: Add, remove, and reorder transformation steps.
Configure Parameters: Adjust settings for each step.
Execute: Run the pipeline and save the result.

title: Transform Widget
text:
Using the Widget

1. Selecting Input
Use the Input Selector at the top of the widget to choose a data item from your project.

When you select data in the Data Manager or other widgets, the Transform Widget will automatically update to focus on that item.
The valid transformation steps available to you depend on the type of data you have selected.



2. Building a Pipeline
The pipeline is a list of steps that run in order.

Add Step: Click the + button or drag a transform from the library (if available) into the step list.
Remove Step: Select a step and click the - button.
Reorder: Drag and drop steps to change their execution order.

Each step transforms the data from the previous step. The widget ensures that the output of one step is compatible with the input of the next.


3. Pre-Reductions (Advanced)
Some transformations require global statistics about the data before they can run. For example, a Z-Score Normalization needs the Mean and Standard Deviation of the entire dataset.

Use the Pre-Reduction Panel to calculate these values.
These values are stored in a temporary “Value Store” and can be bound to the parameters of your transformation steps.



4. Step Configuration
When you select a step in the list, its parameters appear in the Configuration Panel.

Parameters can be simple values (numbers, text) or bindings to Pre-Reduction values.
Adjust these settings to customize the transformation.



5. Execution
Once your pipeline is valid:

Output Name: Enter a name for the result. The widget may suggest one for you.
Execute: Click the Run button.
The result will be created and added to the Data Manager.

title: Remove Small Connected Components
text:
This transform removes small, isolated groups of pixels (connected components) from a binary mask, which is useful for cleaning up noise or irrelevant objects.


In image analysis, particularly with binary masks, it’s common to have small, spurious regions of interest that are not relevant to the main analysis. This transform uses a connected components algorithm to identify all distinct, contiguous regions of pixels in the mask. It then filters out any region whose total number of pixels is below a specified threshold.
This process helps to isolate and preserve only the most significant structures in the mask, making subsequent analysis, such as object tracking or morphological measurement, more robust. The connectivity analysis considers pixels to be connected if they touch at their edges or corners (8-connectivity).
This transform takes a mask as input and produces a new, cleaned-up mask as output.





Calcium Imaging Cleanup: In two-photon or wide-field calcium imaging, masks representing active neurons or regions of interest (ROIs) can be noisy. This transform can remove small, spurious signals that are unlikely to be true neuronal activity, ensuring that only significant ROIs are kept for analysis.
Behavioral Tracking: When tracking an animal’s position or posture using video, the resulting binary masks can contain noise from lighting changes or background artifacts. Removing small connected components can clean up the mask of the animal, leading to more accurate tracking of its centroid or body shape.
Histology and Morphology: When analyzing images of tissue slices, automated segmentation can produce small, artifactual regions. This transform can be used to filter out these artifacts, leaving only the larger, more relevant structures like cell bodies or labeled tracts.

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
1. Calculate Area
What it does: For each timestamp, sums pixel counts across all masks at that time.
If \(\mathcal{M}_t\) is the set of masks at time \(t\) and \(|m|\) is pixel count of mask \(m\):
\[
A_t = \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}_t} |m|
\]
Output: AnalogTimeSeries (time -> total area).
See detailed page: Calculate Mask Area

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
2. Calculate Mask Centroid
What it does: Computes geometric centroid per mask using uniform pixel weighting.
For a mask with points \((x_i, y_i)\), \(i = 1..N\):
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i,
\qquad
\bar{y} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i
\]
Output: PointData (one centroid point per mask instance).
See detailed page: Calculate Mask Centroid

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
3. Calculate Mask Principal Axis
What it does: Computes covariance of mask points, takes the major or minor eigenvector, and emits a line through centroid extended to the mask bounding box.
Covariance terms (sample form):
\[
C_{xx}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2,
\quad
C_{xy}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y}),
\quad
C_{yy}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum (y_i-\bar{y})^2
\]
Eigenvalues of \(\begin{bmatrix}C_{xx} & C_{xy}\\ C_{xy} & C_{yy}\end{bmatrix}\):
\[
\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\operatorname{tr}(C)}{2}
\pm
\sqrt{\left(\frac{C_{xx}-C_{yy}}{2}\right)^2 + C_{xy}^2}
\]
Major axis uses eigenvector of larger \(\lambda\); minor axis uses the orthogonal direction.
Output: LineData.
See detailed page: Calculate Mask Principal Axis

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
4. Remove Small Connected Components
What it does: Converts each mask to a binary image, labels 8-connected components (BFS), and removes components smaller than a threshold.
If component sizes are \(s_k\), keep component \(k\) iff:
\[
s_k \ge \tau
\]
where \(\tau\) is the user threshold.
Output: MaskData.
See detailed page: Remove Small Connected Components

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
5. Fill Mask Holes
What it does: Flood-fills boundary-connected background (4-connectivity) on the inverted mask; unvisited background pixels are holes and are filled.
Let \(M\) be foreground and \(B = \neg M\) background. If \(B_{\text{boundary-connected}}\) are background pixels reachable from the image border, then holes are:
\[
H = B \setminus B_{\text{boundary-connected}}
\]
and filled mask is:
\[
M' = M \cup H
\]
Output: MaskData.
See detailed page: Fill Mask Holes

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
6. Apply Median Filter
What it does: Applies median filtering on the binary mask image with an odd square window and reflection padding.
For window neighborhood \(\mathcal{N}_w(p)\):
\[
M'(p) = \operatorname{median}\{M(q) : q \in \mathcal{N}_w(p)\}
\]
For binary masks, this behaves like a local majority operation.
Output: MaskData.
See detailed page: Apply Median Filter

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
7. Skeletonize Mask
What it does: Iterative LUT-based thinning (adapted from scikit-image) until convergence, preserving topology while reducing regions to a 1-pixel skeleton.
Conceptually:
\[
M^{(k+1)} = T\left(M^{(k)}\right)
\]
where \(T\) removes only pixels marked deletable by neighborhood LUT rules in alternating passes.
Output: MaskData.
See detailed page: Skeletonize Mask

title: Mask Transforms Reference
text:
8. Convert Mask To Line
What it does: Converts each mask to an ordered line using one of two entry strategies:

Skeletonize: skeletonize first, then order points.
NearestToReference: order points directly from mask pixels.

Then applies optional cleanup/smoothing:

Order points by endpoint/reference-aware nearest-neighbor traversal.
Optional outlier removal via parametric polynomial fit.
Optional polynomial smoothing.
Final resampling to target spacing.

Parametric fit uses normalized arc-length \(t \in [0,1]\):
\[
x(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n} a_j t^j,
\qquad
y(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j t^j
\]
Outlier score for point \(i\):
\[
e_i^2 = (x_i-x(t_i))^2 + (y_i-y(t_i))^2
\]
Point is removed if \(e_i^2 > \text{error_threshold}^2\) (equivalently, \(e_i > \text{error_threshold}\)).
Output: LineData.
Status: No dedicated user-guide page yet.

title: Calculate Mask Area
text:
This transform calculates the total area of all detected masks at each point in time, providing a measure of the overall size of masked regions.


This transformation processes a series of masks and, for each timestamp, calculates the total area covered by all masks at that specific time. The area is determined by summing the number of pixels (or voxels) that constitute each mask.
The result is an analog time series where the value at each point in time represents the total mask area for that moment. This is particularly useful for quantifying how the size of a region of interest (ROI) changes over time. Since this operation simply counts pixels within existing masks, it does not require any configuration parameters.
This transform takes a mask series as input and produces an analog time series as output.




In neuroscience research, quantifying the area of specific regions is a common requirement for analyzing imaging data:

Cell Swelling or Shrinking: When studying cellular dynamics, this transform can measure changes in the cross-sectional area of a cell over time, which might occur in response to a stimulus or pathological condition.
Pupilometry: In vision and cognitive neuroscience, tracking the area of the pupil provides insights into arousal, attention, and cognitive load. This transform can be applied to masks of the pupil from eye-tracking videos.
Lesion Sizing: In studies of brain injury or disease, this can be used to quantify the size of a lesion or a plaque from histological or in-vivo imaging data, tracking its progression over time.
Calcium Imaging ROI Activity: For analyzing calcium imaging data, this transform can measure the area of a region of interest (ROI) that shows significant activity (e.g., above a certain brightness threshold), indicating the spatial extent of neural firing.

Line Curvature
text:
This transform calculates the curvature of a 2D line at a specified point. This is useful for analyzing the shape and tortuosity of lines, such as animal trajectories or neuronal processes.


The Line Curvature transform measures how much a line bends at a given point. It does this by fitting a parametric polynomial to the line’s (x, y) coordinates and then calculating the curvature of the fitted polynomial at a user-specified position along the line’s length.
The transform takes a LineData object (representing one or more lines over time) as input and produces an AnalogTimeSeries as output, where each value represents the calculated curvature at the corresponding time point.
This method allows for a smooth and robust estimation of curvature even when the underlying line data is noisy or unevenly sampled.




In neuroscience, analyzing the geometry of paths and structures is crucial for understanding behavior and neural architecture:

Animal Trajectory Analysis: The curvature of an animal’s path (e.g., a rat in a maze) can reveal changes in exploratory strategy, searching behavior, or the effects of neurological manipulations. High curvature might indicate turning or searching, while low curvature suggests straight-line travel.
Neuronal Arborization: When analyzing the structure of neurons from microscope images, the curvature of dendrites or axons can be quantified to characterize their branching patterns and complexity. This is important for studying neuronal development, plasticity, and disease.
Analysis of Saccadic Eye Movements: The trajectory of saccadic eye movements is not perfectly straight. Analyzing the curvature of these paths can provide insights into the underlying motor control mechanisms.

title: Line Curvature
text:
Parameters
This transform has the following parameters:

position: A fractional value between 0.0 and 1.0 indicating the point along the line’s total length at which to calculate the curvature. 0.0 is the start of the line, 0.5 is the midpoint, and 1.0 is the end.
method: The algorithm to use for calculating curvature. Currently, only one option is available:

PolynomialFit: Fits a parametric polynomial to the line data and calculates the analytical curvature.

polynomial_order: The order of the polynomial to fit to the line data. A higher order can capture more complex curves but may be more sensitive to noise. A minimum of 2 is required for curvature calculation.
fitting_window_percentage: The percentage (from 0.0 to 1.0) of the total line length to use for the polynomial fit, centered on the position parameter. A smaller window focuses the curvature calculation on the local shape, while a larger window provides a more global measure.

title: Line Curvature
Line Angle
text:
This transform calculates the angle of a line at a specific position along its length for each point in time.


The Line Angle transform provides a way to quantify the orientation of a line in a 2D space. This can be particularly useful for analyzing the movement or orientation of objects that are tracked as lines. The angle is measured relative to a customizable reference vector, which defaults to the positive x-axis (0 degrees).
There are two methods for calculating the angle:

Direct Points: This method approximates the tangent at a given position by calculating the angle of the vector between the point at that position and the point immediately preceding it. This is a simple and fast method suitable for getting a local orientation.
Polynomial Fit: This method fits a polynomial of a given order to the line’s points (parameterized by their cumulative distance). The angle is then calculated from the derivative of the polynomial at the specified position. This method can provide a more accurate estimate of the tangent angle at a specific point along a curved line.





In neuroscience, this transform can be used to analyze a variety of data:

Whisker Tracking: The angle of a tracked whisker relative to the animal’s head can be calculated to study sensory input and motor control.
Limb Tracking: The angle of a limb segment (e.g., the forearm) can be calculated to analyze reaching movements or other motor behaviors.
Tongue Tracking: The angle of the tongue during licking or other oral movements can be quantified.

title: Line Angle
text:
Parameters
This transform has the following parameters:

position: A value between 0.0 and 1.0 that specifies the point along the line at which to calculate the angle. For example, 0.5 would be the midpoint of the line.
method: The calculation method to use.

Direct Points: (Default) Calculates the angle based on the vector from the start of the line to the point at position.
Polynomial Fit: Fits a polynomial to the line and calculates the angle from the derivative.

polynomial_order: The order of the polynomial to fit to the line when using the Polynomial Fit method. A higher order can capture more complex curves but requires more points and can be prone to overfitting. A typical value is 2 or 3.
reference_x: The x-component of the reference vector. Defaults to 1.0.
reference_y: The y-component of the reference vector. Defaults to 0.0. The default vector (1.0, 0.0) corresponds to the positive x-axis, meaning angles are measured with 0 degrees pointing to the right.

title: Line Angle
Fill Mask Holes
text:
This transform fills any enclosed holes within binary mask regions, which is useful for creating solid,contiguous masks from outlines or noisy data.


In image analysis, particularly with masks derived from object detection or segmentation, it’s common to have “holes” – background areas completely surrounded by foreground. This transform identifies and fills these holes.
The process works by identifying all background regions that are not connected to the edges of the image. Any such isolated background region is considered a hole and is filled in, effectively becoming part of the foreground mask. This is useful for cleaning up masks to ensure that objects are represented as solid shapes, which is often a prerequisite for accurate area, centroid, or morphological analysis.





Cell Body Segmentation: When segmenting neurons from imaging data, the detected outline of a cell might not be perfectly filled. This transform can be used to fill the interior of the cell body, ensuring it’s a solid mask for subsequent analysis like measuring cell size or fluorescence intensity.
Receptive Field Mapping: In studies mapping receptive fields, a mask might be generated that outlines the field but contains small gaps or holes. Filling these holes can create a more accurate and solid representation of the receptive field.
Lesion Analysis: When analyzing images of tissue lesions, this transform can help create solid masks of the lesion areas, even if the initial segmentation is imperfect, allowing for more accurate measurement of lesion volume or area.

Extract Line Subsegment
text:
This transform extracts a portion of a line (a subsegment) based on specified start and end points.


This transformation allows for the precise extraction of a subsegment from a series of lines, such as those representing the movement of a tracked object over time. You can define the start and end of the subsegment as a fraction of the total line length. For example, you can extract the middle 50% of a line.
This is particularly useful for focusing analysis on a specific part of a trajectory or shape. For instance, in neuroscience, you might use this to analyze the movement of an animal’s limb, focusing only on the part of the movement where the limb is closest to a target.

The extraction can be done in two ways:

Direct: This method pulls the original points from the line that fall within the specified subsegment. This is fast and preserves the original data points.
Parametric: This method fits a polynomial to the line and then generates a new, smooth subsegment with a specified number of points. This is useful for standardizing the length and spacing of the subsegment for further analysis, such as comparing shapes across different trials.





Whisker Tracking: When analyzing whisker movements, you might want to extract only the portion of the whisker closest to an object it’s exploring.
Limb Tracking: In studies of motor control, you could extract the segment of a limb’s trajectory during a specific phase of a reach-to-grasp movement.
Neural Arborization: When analyzing the structure of neurons, this transform could be used to isolate specific dendritic or axonal segments for morphological analysis.

title: Extract Line Subsegment
text:
Parameters
This transform has the following parameters:

start_position: The starting point of the subsegment, as a fraction of the total line length (from 0.0 to 1.0).
end_position: The ending point of the subsegment, as a fraction of the total line length (from 0.0 to 1.0).
method: The extraction method to use. This can be:

Direct: Directly extracts the original points within the subsegment range.
Parametric: Uses polynomial interpolation to create a new, smooth subsegment.

polynomial_order: (Parametric method only) The order of the polynomial to fit to the line. A higher order can capture more complex curves but may also be more sensitive to noise.
output_points: (Parametric method only) The number of points to generate in the output subsegment.
preserve_original_spacing: (Direct method only) If true, the subsegment will consist of the original points from the line that fall within the specified range. If false, the subsegment will be resampled to have evenly spaced points.

Calculate Mask Principal Axis
text:
This transform calculates the principal axis of a mask, which is a line that represents the primary orientation of the shape defined by the mask’s pixels.


This [Data Transform Operation] is used to determine the orientation of objects within a mask. It analyzes the distribution of pixels in a mask to find its principal axes. The major axis represents the longest dimension of the shape, indicating its primary orientation, while the minor axis is perpendicular to the major axis and represents the shortest dimension.
This is useful for quantifying the orientation of elongated objects. The output is a line segment that passes through the centroid of the mask and aligns with either the major or minor axis of pixel variance.





Cellular Morphology: In microscopy images, this can be used to quantify the orientation of cells, such as neurons or glia, which can be important for understanding tissue organization and cell migration.
Behavioral Analysis: When tracking the posture of an animal, the principal axis of a body part’s mask (like a limb or tail) can provide a quantitative measure of its angle and movement over time.
Object Interaction: It can be used to determine how an animal is oriented relative to an object in its environment, for example, by calculating the principal axis of the animal’s body mask.

text:

Major: The axis of greatest variance (the “longest” direction of the shape).
Minor: The axis of least variance (the “shortest” direction of the shape), perpendicular to the major axis.

Apply Median Filter
text:
This transform applies a median filter to a binary mask, which is effective at removing “salt-and-pepper” noise and smoothing object boundaries.


The median filter is a non-linear digital filtering technique used to remove noise from an image or signal. For each pixel in the mask, the filter considers a square neighborhood of a specified size around it, finds the median of all the pixel values in that neighborhood, and replaces the central pixel with that median value.
This process is highly effective at removing isolated pixels of one color surrounded by pixels of another color (i.e., “salt-and-pepper” noise). It is also good at preserving sharp edges in the image while smoothing out noise, making it preferable to a standard blurring (mean) filter in many cases.
The figure below illustrates how the median filter removes isolated black and white pixels from a binary mask. Notice how a larger window size results in more aggressive smoothing.




In neuroscience, image processing is often a critical step in data analysis. The median filter is a valuable tool for pre-processing image-based data.

Calcium Imaging Analysis: When segmenting active neurons from calcium imaging videos, the resulting binary masks can be noisy. A median filter can clean up these masks before further analysis, such as calculating cell centroids or areas, leading to more accurate results.
Morphological Reconstruction: After tracing neurons from microscopy images, digital reconstructions can have small artifacts. Applying a median filter to a 2D projection (mask) of the reconstruction can help remove these artifacts before measuring morphological properties.
Whisker Tracking: In behavioral neuroscience, tracking the position of an animal’s whiskers often produces binary images of the whisker. A median filter can smooth the whisker’s shape and remove spurious pixels from the background, improving the accuracy of tracking algorithms.

Name

Analog Hilbert Phase
text:
This transform calculates the instantaneous phase of an analog signal, which is useful for analyzing oscillations.


The Hilbert transform is a mathematical operation that shifts the phase of all positive frequency components of a signal by -90 degrees and all negative frequency components by +90 degrees. When this phase-shifted signal (the imaginary part) is combined with the original signal (the real part), it forms a complex-valued “analytic signal”.
The instantaneous phase is the angle of this complex number at each point in time. It provides a way to represent an oscillating signal in terms of its phase, which progresses from -π to +π for each cycle of the oscillation. This transform uses an efficient FFT-based method to compute the Hilbert transform.





In neuroscience, analyzing the phase of neural signals is crucial for understanding brain function. Some common applications include:

Rhythmic Behaviors: The phase of signals from sensors tracking rhythmic behaviors like whisking, sniffing, or licking can be extracted to correlate them with neural activity.

title: Analog Hilbert Phase
text:
Parameters
This transform has the following parameters:

low_frequency: The low-cut frequency for the bandpass filter, in Hertz. This determines the lower end of the frequency range you want to analyze.
high_frequency: The high-cut frequency for the bandpass filter, in Hertz. This determines the upper end of the frequency range you want to analyze.

Analog Event Threshold
text:
This transform detects moments in time (events) when an analog signal crosses a specified value, which is useful for identifying significant occurrences in the data.


Thresholding is a fundamental method for event detection in time-series data. This operation identifies every point in time where the signal’s amplitude crosses a defined threshold in a specific direction (either rising above it, falling below it, or crossing it in either direction).
A “lockout” period can also be set. After an event is detected, the algorithm will ignore any further threshold crossings for the duration of this period, which helps prevent a single, noisy event from being counted multiple times.
This transform takes an analog time series as input and produces a digital event series as output, where each event corresponds to a single point in time when a threshold crossing was detected.





In neuroscience, thresholding is a common technique for identifying meaningful events in continuous data streams:

Spike Detection: In extracellular recordings, thresholding can be used to identify action potentials (spikes) that stand out from the background noise. A lockout time is critical here to avoid detecting the same spike multiple times as it repolarizes.
Behavioral Event Marking: For data from sensors like accelerometers or force transducers, thresholding can mark the onset of specific behaviors, such as a mouse starting to run on a wheel or a bird pecking a key.
Calcium Imaging Analysis: In calcium imaging data, which reflects neural activity, thresholding can be used to detect significant calcium transients that indicate a neuron or a group of neurons are firing.

title: Analog Event Threshold
text:
This transform detects moments in time (events) when an analog signal crosses a specified value, which is useful for identifying significant occurrences in the data.


Thresholding is a fundamental method for event detection in time-series data. This operation identifies every point in time where the signal’s amplitude crosses a defined threshold in a specific direction (either rising above it, falling below it, or crossing it in either direction).
A “lockout” period can also be set. After an event is detected, the algorithm will ignore any further threshold crossings for the duration of this period, which helps prevent a single, noisy event from being counted multiple times.
This transform takes an analog time series as input and produces a digital event series as output, where each event corresponds to a single point in time when a threshold crossing was detected.





In neuroscience, thresholding is a common technique for identifying meaningful events in continuous data streams:

Spike Detection: In extracellular recordings, thresholding can be used to identify action potentials (spikes) that stand out from the background noise. A lockout time is critical here to avoid detecting the same spike multiple times as it repolarizes.
Behavioral Event Marking: For data from sensors like accelerometers or force transducers, thresholding can mark the onset of specific behaviors, such as a mouse starting to run on a wheel or a bird pecking a key.
Calcium Imaging Analysis: In calcium imaging data, which reflects neural activity, thresholding can be used to detect significant calcium transients that indicate a neuron or a group of neurons are firing.

title: Analog Event Threshold
text:
Parameters
This transform has the following parameters:

threshold_value: The amplitude value the signal must cross to be considered an event.
direction: Specifies the direction of the crossing required to trigger an event. This can be:

Positive (Rising): An event is detected when the signal crosses the threshold from a lower to a higher value.
Negative (Falling): An event is detected when the signal crosses the threshold from a higher to a lower value.
Absolute: An event is detected whenever the absolute value of the signal crosses the threshold value (useful for detecting deviations from baseline in either direction).

lockout_time: A duration (in the same time units as the data, e.g., seconds) after each detected event during which no new events will be registered. This is useful for preventing multiple detections of a single, noisy event.

title: Video Loading
text:
Technical Details

Frame Decoding
Neuralyzer optimizes video playback using these strategies:

Sequential access: When playing forward, frames decode sequentially without seeking
Keyframe seeking: For random access (scrubbing, jumping), the decoder seeks to the nearest keyframe
Large jumps: Forward jumps greater than 100 frames trigger keyframe seeking



Display Formats
Videos can be displayed in:

Grayscale (Gray) - Single channel, 8-bit
Color (Color) - ARGB, 32-bit

The display format affects how the video is processed and rendered but does not modify the source file.


Memory Considerations
Only the current frame is held in memory. Large videos (4K, long duration) are handled efficiently since the entire video is not loaded at once.

title: Intan
text: Intan Technologies acquisition systems are commonly used for electrophysiology. The system saves data in several files, with amplifier.dat and digitalin.dat being the primary files for analog and digital data, respectively.

title: Intan
text:
File Formats

amplifier.dat
The amplifier.dat file contains the analog data from the amplifier channels. - Format: 2D array of int16 values. - Organization: Time-major (all channels at t=0, then all channels at t=1, etc.). - Conversion: The values be converted to microvolts using a bit resolution of 0.196 µV/bit. - Sampling Rate: Typically 30 kHz.


digitalin.dat
The digitalin.dat file contains digital input data. - Format: Binary file with one uint16 value per sampling tick. - Content: Each bit of the uint16 value represents a high (1) or low (0) state for a specific digital input channel.

title: Intan
text:
Loading Data
Data can be loaded using JSON configuration objects. Below are examples for common loading scenarios.

Loading Analog Time Series
To load amplifier.dat as an analog time series:
{
    "filepath": "amplifier.dat",
    "data_type": "analog",
    "name": "voltage",
    "format": "int16",
    "header_size": 0,
    "channel_count": 32,
    "clock": "master",
    "use_memory_mapped": true
}


Loading Digital Interval Series
To load a specific digital input (e.g., channel 0) as a series of intervals:
{
    "filepath": "digitalin.dat",
    "data_type": "digital_interval",
    "name": "pico",
    "format": "uint16",
    "channel": 0,
    "transition": "rising",
    "clock": "master",
    "header_size": 0
}


Creating a TimeFrame from Digital Input
If a digital input represents a time reference (e.g., channel 1):
{
    "filepath": "digitalin.dat",
    "data_type": "time",
    "name": "time",
    "format": "uint16",
    "channel": 1,
    "transition": "rising"
}


Creating a TimeFrame from Total Samples
To create a TimeFrame based on the total number of samples in the file:
{
    "filepath": "digitalin.dat",
    "data_type": "time",
    "name": "master",
    "format": "uint16_length"
}

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
This guide walks through fitting a GLM-HMM (Generalized Linear Model–Hidden Markov Model) to classify whisker contact frames using deep-learning encoder features and the ssm library.
A standard HMM models contact/no-contact as hidden states emitting high-dimensional features from a Gaussian distribution. At high frame rates this struggles because (1) the transition matrix is overwhelmingly self-transitioning, (2) full covariance in 192 dimensions is underdetermined without enormous data, and (3) the transition dynamics cannot adapt to the feature context.
A GLM-HMM with input-driven observations (Ashwood et al., 2022) solves these problems. Instead of modelling the features as emissions, it treats them as inputs to a per-state logistic regression that predicts a binary contact label:
\[
P(y_t = \text{contact} \mid z_t = k,\; \mathbf{u}_t) =
\sigma(\mathbf{w}_k^\top \mathbf{u}_t)
\]
Each state \(k\) has its own weight vector \(\mathbf{w}_k\), so different states capture different feature→contact relationships (e.g., pole-present vs. pole-absent dynamics). The hidden states are discovered by EM.

Pipeline
Encoder Features (TensorData)       Contact Labels (DigitalIntervalSeries)
        │                                         │
        │  inputs u_t ∈ ℝ^D                       │  observations y_t ∈ {0,1}
        ▼                                         ▼

  │                   GLM-HMM (ssm)                   │
  │                                                   │

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Step 1: Extract Data from DataManager
import numpy as np
import whisker_toolbox as wt

dm = wt.DataManager()

# --- Encoder features: shape (T, D) ---
features_td = dm.getData("features")          # TensorData
X_all = np.array(features_td.values, copy=True)  # writable copy
T_total, D = X_all.shape
print(f"Feature matrix: {T_total} frames × {D} dimensions")

# --- Training block intervals ---
train_intervals = dm.getData("train").toList()
print(f"Training blocks: {len(train_intervals)}")
for iv in train_intervals:
    print(f"  [{iv.start}, {iv.end})")

# --- Contact intervals ---
contact_intervals = dm.getData("contact").toList()
print(f"Contact intervals: {len(contact_intervals)}")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
text:
Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
We need a frame-level binary label vector \(y_t \in \{0, 1\}\) for each training block. ssm expects a list of sessions (one array per training block).
def intervals_to_binary(total_frames, intervals):
    """Convert a list of Interval objects to a binary array of shape (total_frames,)."""
    labels = np.zeros(total_frames, dtype=int)
    for iv in intervals:
        labels[iv.start:iv.end] = 1
    return labels

# Build per-frame binary contact labels over the entire session
y_all = intervals_to_binary(T_total, contact_intervals)

# Split into per-block arrays (ssm expects a list of sessions)
X_blocks = []  # list of (T_block, D) arrays — inputs
y_blocks = []  # list of (T_block, 1) arrays — observations

for iv in train_intervals:
    s, e = int(iv.start), int(iv.end)
    X_blocks.append(X_all[s:e])
    # ssm requires observations shape (T, obs_dim) with obs_dim=1
    y_blocks.append(y_all[s:e].reshape(-1, 1))

print(f"Prepared {len(X_blocks)} training blocks")
for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(zip(X_blocks, y_blocks)):
    n_contact = yb.sum()
    print(f"  Block {i}: {len(yb)} frames, {n_contact} contact ({100*n_contact/len(yb):.1f}%)")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Step 3: Create the GLM-HMM
import ssm

num_states = 3         # K: number of hidden behavioral states
obs_dim = 1            # y_t is scalar (binary contact label)
num_categories = 2     # binary outcome: contact / no-contact
input_dim = D          # encoder feature dimensionality

glmhmm = ssm.HMM(
    num_states,
    obs_dim,
    input_dim,
    observations="input_driven_obs",
    observation_kwargs=dict(C=num_categories),
    transitions="standard",
)
print(f"GLM-HMM: {num_states} states, {input_dim}-dim inputs, {num_categories} categories")

Choosing the number of states

K=2 is the minimum: one state for “contact-responsive” frames and one for “non-responsive”.
K=3 is recommended: adds a transition/ambiguous state that absorbs boundary uncertainty.
Higher K may overfit; use cross-validation (see Step 6) to select.



MAP estimation (optional)
If data is limited, add a prior to regularise the GLM weights:
prior_sigma = 2    # Gaussian prior σ on GLM weights
prior_alpha = 2    # Dirichlet prior α on transition rows

glmhmm_map = ssm.HMM(
    num_states,
    obs_dim,
    input_dim,
    observations="input_driven_obs",
    observation_kwargs=dict(C=num_categories, prior_sigma=prior_sigma),
    transitions="sticky",
    transition_kwargs=dict(alpha=prior_alpha, kappa=0),
)

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
text:
Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
N_iters = 200      # max EM iterations
tolerance = 1e-4   # stop early if LL improvement < tolerance

fit_ll = glmhmm.fit(
    y_blocks,
    inputs=X_blocks,
    method="em",
    num_iters=N_iters,
    tolerance=tolerance,
)
print(f"Final log-likelihood: {fit_ll[-1]:.2f}")

Multiple initialisations
EM finds a local optimum. Run several random initialisations and keep the best:
best_ll = -np.inf
best_model = None

for init in range(5):
    candidate = ssm.HMM(
        num_states, obs_dim, input_dim,
        observations="input_driven_obs",
        observation_kwargs=dict(C=num_categories),
        transitions="standard",
    )
    ll = candidate.fit(y_blocks, inputs=X_blocks, method="em",
                       num_iters=N_iters, tolerance=tolerance)
    if ll[-1] > best_ll:
        best_ll = ll[-1]
        best_model = candidate

glmhmm = best_model
print(f"Best log-likelihood across initialisations: {best_ll:.2f}")


Plot convergence
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.plot(fit_ll)
ax.set_xlabel("EM Iteration")
ax.set_ylabel("Log Probability")
ax.set_title("GLM-HMM Training Convergence")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Step 5: Decode and Inspect

Viterbi decoding (most likely state sequence)
# Decode each training block
for i, (yb, xb) in enumerate(zip(y_blocks, X_blocks)):
    states = glmhmm.most_likely_states(yb, input=xb)
    print(f"Block {i}: states = {np.unique(states, return_counts=True)}")


Posterior state probabilities
posterior_probs = [
    glmhmm.expected_states(data=yb, input=xb)[0]
    for yb, xb in zip(y_blocks, X_blocks)
]

# Plot posterior for the first block
fig, axes = plt.subplots(num_states + 1, 1, figsize=(10, 2 * (num_states + 1)),
                         sharex=True)
block_idx = 0
for k in range(num_states):
    axes[k].plot(posterior_probs[block_idx][:, k], label=f"State {k+1}")
    axes[k].set_ylabel(f"P(z={k+1})")
    axes[k].set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)

axes[-1].plot(y_blocks[block_idx], color="black", alpha=0.5)
axes[-1].set_ylabel("Contact label")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Frame (within block)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Inspect learned transition matrix
trans_mat = np.exp(glmhmm.transitions.log_Ps)
print("Transition matrix:")
print(np.around(trans_mat, decimals=3))


Inspect per-state GLM weights
weights = glmhmm.observations.params  # shape (K, C-1, input_dim)
for k in range(num_states):
    w = weights[k, 0, :]  # weight vector for state k (C-1 = 1 for binary)
    print(f"State {k+1}: ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}, "
          f"top-5 features = {np.argsort(np.abs(w))[-5:][::-1]}")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 6: Predict Contact on Unlabeled Data
text:
Step 6: Predict Contact on Unlabeled Data
After training, we can predict frame-level contact probability on new data where labels are unavailable. The key insight is that the per-state GLM weights give \(P(y=1 \mid z_t=k,\; \mathbf{u}_t)\) and the transition model gives \(P(z_t \mid z_{t-1})\).
We use forward filtering to compute \(P(z_t \mid \mathbf{u}_{1:t})\) and then marginalise over states:
\[
P(y_t = 1 \mid \mathbf{u}_{1:t}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K}
P(y_t = 1 \mid z_t = k, \mathbf{u}_t)\;
P(z_t = k \mid \mathbf{u}_{1:t})
\]
from scipy.special import expit  # sigmoid function


def predict_contact(glmhmm, X_new):
    """Predict per-frame contact probability on unlabeled data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    glmhmm : ssm.HMM
        Fitted GLM-HMM with input_driven_obs observations.
    X_new : np.ndarray, shape (T, D)
        Encoder features for the prediction segment.

    Returns
    -------
    contact_prob : np.ndarray, shape (T,)
        P(contact) per frame.
    state_probs : np.ndarray, shape (T, K)
        Forward-filtered state probabilities.
    """
    K = glmhmm.K
    T_pred = X_new.shape[0]

    # Extract model parameters
    log_pi0 = glmhmm.init_state_distn.log_initial_state_distn(X_new)  # (K,)
    log_A = glmhmm.transitions.log_Ps  # (K, K)
    A = np.exp(log_A)
    weights = glmhmm.observations.params  # (K, C-1, D)

    # Per-state contact probability: P(y=1 | z=k, u_t) = sigmoid(w_k^T u_t)
    # weights shape: (K, 1, D) for binary case
    logits = X_new @ weights[:, 0, :].T  # (T, K)
    p_contact_given_state = expit(logits)  # (T, K)

    # Forward filtering (no observation updates — we don't have labels)
    alpha = np.exp(log_pi0)  # (K,)
    alpha = alpha / alpha.sum()

    state_probs = np.zeros((T_pred, K))
    state_probs[0] = alpha

    for t in range(1, T_pred):
        alpha = alpha @ A  # predict: (K,) @ (K,K) = (K,)
        alpha = alpha / alpha.sum()
        state_probs[t] = alpha

    # Marginalise: P(y=1 | u_{1:t}) = sum_k P(y=1|z=k, u_t) * P(z=k)
    contact_prob = np.sum(p_contact_given_state * state_probs, axis=1)

    return contact_prob, state_probs

Apply to a validation segment
# Use frames outside training blocks as validation
val_start = int(train_intervals[-1].end)  # after last training block
val_end = min(val_start + 5000, T_total)  # up to 5000 frames
X_val = X_all[val_start:val_end]

contact_prob, state_probs = predict_contact(glmhmm, X_val)

# Threshold to get binary predictions
threshold = 0.5
y_pred = (contact_prob >= threshold).astype(int)
print(f"Predicted {y_pred.sum()} contact frames out of {len(y_pred)}")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 7: Convert Predictions to Intervals and Write Back
text:
Step 7: Convert Predictions to Intervals and Write Back
def binary_to_intervals(y_pred, offset=0):
    """Convert a binary prediction array to a list of (start, end) tuples.

    Parameters
    ----------
    y_pred : np.ndarray, shape (T,)
        Binary predictions (0 or 1).
    offset : int
        Frame offset to add (e.g., if y_pred starts from frame val_start).

    Returns
    -------
    intervals : list of (int, int)
        Each tuple is (start_frame, end_frame) of a contiguous contact block.
    """
    intervals = []
    in_interval = False
    start = 0
    for t in range(len(y_pred)):
        if y_pred[t] == 1 and not in_interval:
            start = t + offset
            in_interval = True
        elif y_pred[t] == 0 and in_interval:
            intervals.append((start, t + offset))
            in_interval = False
    if in_interval:
        intervals.append((start, len(y_pred) + offset))
    return intervals

# Convert to intervals
pred_intervals = binary_to_intervals(y_pred, offset=val_start)
print(f"Predicted {len(pred_intervals)} contact intervals")

# Write back to DataManager
result = wt.DigitalIntervalSeries()
for s, e in pred_intervals:
    result.addInterval(s, e)

time_key = dm.getTimeKey("features")
dm.setData("glm_hmm_contact", result, time_key)
print("Wrote 'glm_hmm_contact' to DataManager")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Cross-Validation
To select \(K\) and evaluate prediction quality, hold out one training block at a time:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score

def cross_validate(K, X_blocks, y_blocks, n_init=5, n_iters=200, tol=1e-4):
    """Leave-one-block-out cross-validation for GLM-HMM."""
    f1_scores = []
    for held_out in range(len(X_blocks)):
        X_train = [X_blocks[i] for i in range(len(X_blocks)) if i != held_out]
        y_train = [y_blocks[i] for i in range(len(y_blocks)) if i != held_out]

        best_ll = -np.inf
        best_m = None
        for _ in range(n_init):
            m = ssm.HMM(K, 1, D,
                        observations="input_driven_obs",
                        observation_kwargs=dict(C=2),
                        transitions="standard")
            ll = m.fit(y_train, inputs=X_train, method="em",
                       num_iters=n_iters, tolerance=tol)
            if ll[-1] > best_ll:
                best_ll = ll[-1]
                best_m = m

        # Predict on held-out block
        prob, _ = predict_contact(best_m, X_blocks[held_out])
        y_pred = (prob >= 0.5).astype(int)
        y_true = y_blocks[held_out].ravel()
        f1_scores.append(f1_score(y_true, y_pred))

    return np.mean(f1_scores), np.std(f1_scores)

for K in [2, 3, 4]:
    mean_f1, std_f1 = cross_validate(K, X_blocks, y_blocks)
    print(f"K={K}: F1 = {mean_f1:.3f} ± {std_f1:.3f}")

text:
Troubleshooting








Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




EM converges but states are degenerate (one state used 99%)
Bad initialisation
Run more random initialisations (n_init ≥ 10)


Log-likelihood decreases
Numerical overflow in 192-dim logistic regression
Standardise features: X = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)


Fit is very slow
Too many features for the GLM
Reduce D via PCA before fitting


Poor F1 on held-out blocks
Too few/many states, or insufficient data
Try different K; use MAP estimation with prior_sigma=2
