title: TimeFrame Resampling & Upsampling Roadmap
text:
Neural data is often recorded at different sampling rates on a shared master clock. A camera might sample at 500 Hz while electrophysiology runs at 30 kHz. To precisely align these signals, the lower-rate data must be upsampled using band-limited interpolation (sinc/Nyquist reconstruction).
Today, the system has no support for:

Creating upsampled TimeFrames from existing ones
Assigning transform output to a different TimeKey than the input
Sinc interpolation as a data transform

Additionally, the pipeline executor has a latent bug: storeOutputData() hardcodes TimeKey("default") instead of propagating the input’s TimeKey.


Transforms are pure data operations. TimeFrame management is the user’s responsibility.
A sinc interpolation transform takes N input samples and an upsampling factor, and produces (N-1) * factor + 1 output samples. It does not create, register, or reference any TimeFrame. The user creates the target TimeFrame beforehand (via the DataManager widget), and the pipeline executor validates that the output size matches the target TimeFrame’s entry count.
This separation has concrete benefits:

Multi-channel efficiency: 4 tetrode channels sharing a TimeFrame are each upsampled independently, but all point at the same pre-created target TimeFrame. No redundant TimeFrame creation.
No DataManager coupling in transforms: transforms remain testable as pure functions with no DataManager dependency.
Clear contract: if the output sample count does not match the target TimeFrame size, the pipeline step fails with an explicit error.




1. User action (DataManager widget):
   "Create Upsampled TimeFrame"
   → Source: camera_time (500 Hz, 1000 entries)
   → Factor: 4
   → New key: camera_time_4x (3997 entries)

2. Pipeline step 1:  SincInterpolation on ch1, output_time_key: camera_time_4x
3. Pipeline step 2:  SincInterpolation on ch2, output_time_key: camera_time_4x
4. Pipeline step 3:  SincInterpolation on ch3, output_time_key: camera_time_4x
5. Pipeline step 4:  SincInterpolation on ch4, output_time_key: camera_time_4x

Contract: each output must have exactly 3997 samples, matching camera_time_4x.

struct DerivedTimeFrameFromUpsamplingOptions {
    std::shared_ptr<TimeFrame> source_timeframe;  ///< TimeFrame to upsample
    int upsampling_factor;                        ///< Integer factor (must be > 0)
};



std::shared_ptr<TimeFrame> createUpsampledTimeFrame(
    DerivedTimeFrameFromUpsamplingOptions const & options);
Behavior:
Given a source TimeFrame with N entries and clock values [t_0, t_1, ..., t_{N-1}], produce a new TimeFrame with (N-1) * factor + 1 entries by linearly interpolating between consecutive pairs:
Source: [0, 60, 120], factor = 4
Output: [0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, 120]
         ↑              ↑                   ↑
       original       original            original

Between t_i and t_{i+1}, insert factor - 1 evenly spaced values.
Values are int — non-integer interpolation results are rounded to the nearest tick.
Factor = 1 returns a copy of the source TimeFrame.
Empty or single-entry source returns a copy (no interpolation possible).

title: TimeFrame Resampling & Upsampling Roadmap
text:
Goal: Implement band-limited (Nyquist) interpolation as a pure data container transform.


For each output sample position m in [0, M-1] where M = (N-1) * factor + 1:

Compute the fractional input position: x = m / factor
For each input sample n in the kernel window [floor(x) - K, floor(x) + K]:

Compute sinc(x - n) weighted by the window function

Output sample = weighted sum of input samples

Where K = kernel_half_width and sinc(t) = sin(πt) / (πt) (with sinc(0) = 1).
At signal boundaries, symmetric extension reflects the input signal to avoid edge artifacts.



enum class SincWindowType { Lanczos, Hann, Blackman };
enum class BoundaryMode { SymmetricExtension, ZeroPad };

struct SincInterpolationParams {
    int upsampling_factor;                                        ///< Required, > 1
    std::optional<int> kernel_half_width;                         ///< Default: 8
    std::optional<SincWindowType> window_type;                    ///< Default: Lanczos
    std::optional<BoundaryMode> boundary_mode;                    ///< Default: SymmetricExtension
};



std::shared_ptr<AnalogTimeSeries> sincInterpolation(
    AnalogTimeSeries const & input,
    SincInterpolationParams const & params,
    ComputeContext const & ctx);

Input: N samples
Output: (N-1) * factor + 1 samples with Dense TimeIndexStorage starting from 0
No TimeFrame access — purely operates on data values




In RegisteredTransforms.cpp:
auto const register_sinc = RegisterContainerTransform<
    AnalogTimeSeries, AnalogTimeSeries, SincInterpolationParams>(
    "SincInterpolation",
    sincInterpolation,
    ContainerTransformMetadata{
        .name = "SincInterpolation",
        .description = "Band-limited sinc interpolation (Nyquist upsampling)",
        .category = "Signal Processing"
    });

title: Testing
text:
Testing makes sure that our code works as expected, and that future changes do not break existing functionality.

Testing Guidelines

Testing is performed with Catch2. 
The component being tested generally has two TEST_CASE parts. The first will test the “happy path” to ensure that the computations work as expected. Different SECTIONs will be used for different computations. A second TEST_CASE will handle error handling and edge cases. Each SECTION will be for a different edge case / error.
Use descriptive names for each test.
TEST_CASES should also use useful tags.
Use REQUIRE instead of CHECK
Simple setup can be performed in the beginning of a TEST_CASE. Fixtures are only necessary for complex setup/teardown.
Prefer Catch::Matchers::WithinRel to Catch::Approx
Test files are included in the same folder as a given translation unit. They should have the same name as the header file with the extension “.test.cpp”. For example mask_to_line.hpp and mask_to_line.cpp will have the test file mask_to_line.test.cpp.

title: Tensor Transform Library — Design Roadmap
text:
Last updated: 2026-03-29


TensorData is the richest numeric container in WhiskerToolbox, supporting 2D matrices, 3D cubes, and N-dimensional arrays across multiple storage backends (Armadillo, Dense, LibTorch). Many scientific workflows require tensor-in → tensor-out operations: dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP), spectral decomposition (SVD, NMF), normalization, slicing, and reshaping. These transforms differ from element-level transforms because:

Shape-dependence — A PCA requires 2D; a conv-filter might need 3D.
Whole-container semantics — Operates on the entire matrix, not element-by-element.
Output shape differs from input — PCA(N×D) → (N×K) where K < D.
Shared state — Some algorithms produce fitted models reusable for projection.





The primary motivating use case is the encoder → embedding → visualization → interaction loop:

  │  DataTransform_Widget or MLCore Dim Reduction tab

  │  ScatterPlotWidget: X=PC1, Y=PC2, color-by-group
  ▼

  │  User selects cluster → entity group created
  ▼

title: Tensor Transform Library — Design Roadmap
text:
TensorData is the richest numeric container in WhiskerToolbox, supporting 2D matrices, 3D cubes, and N-dimensional arrays across multiple storage backends (Armadillo, Dense, LibTorch). Many scientific workflows require tensor-in → tensor-out operations: dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP), spectral decomposition (SVD, NMF), normalization, slicing, and reshaping. These transforms differ from element-level transforms because:

Shape-dependence — A PCA requires 2D; a conv-filter might need 3D.
Whole-container semantics — Operates on the entire matrix, not element-by-element.
Output shape differs from input — PCA(N×D) → (N×K) where K < D.
Shared state — Some algorithms produce fitted models reusable for projection.

title: State Estimation Library
text:
The primary goals of this library are to provide a modular framework for state estimation tasks. The high-level objectives include:

Generate Smooth Estimates: Produce a smooth estimate of a state from raw data.
Compare and Validate: Generate a smooth estimate and compare it against a pre-existing estimate, with the ability to flag potential outliers.
Interpolate Missing Data: Generate smoothed predictions that can fill in gaps where data is missing. This is in contrast to simply refining existing measurements.
Assign Identity to Unlabeled Data: Use predictions to assign identities to measured data points within a time series that has only sparse labels.

title: State Estimation Library
text:
The primary goals of this library are to provide a modular framework for state estimation tasks. The high-level objectives include:

Generate Smooth Estimates: Produce a smooth estimate of a state from raw data.
Compare and Validate: Generate a smooth estimate and compare it against a pre-existing estimate, with the ability to flag potential outliers.
Interpolate Missing Data: Generate smoothed predictions that can fill in gaps where data is missing. This is in contrast to simply refining existing measurements.
Assign Identity to Unlabeled Data: Use predictions to assign identities to measured data points within a time series that has only sparse labels.

title: State Estimation Library
text:
Design Principles and Variation Points
The library should be designed in a modular fashion to accommodate several key points of variation in state estimation problems. The interfaces should be flexible enough to handle significant structural differences between algorithms.

Data Type
The nature of the input data is a primary variation point. The library must handle:

Continuous Data: Analog time series or other continuous state variables.
Discrete Data: Data that exists on a discrete grid or set of points. An example would be making a prediction for a point within an image mask where only certain pixels are available.



Filtering Schemes
The design must support different families of filtering algorithms, which may have different assumptions about data distributions and different methodological considerations.

Kalman Filters:

Standard Kalman Filter
Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for linearized systems
Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)

Particle Filters:

Bootstrap Particle Filter
Sequential Importance Sampling with Resampling (SIR)




Smoothing Operations
Alongside forward-in-time filtering, the library must incorporate smoothing operations, which use the full dataset to refine estimates by making a backward pass through the data. The design should recognize that some smoothers are tightly paired with specific filters, while others may be more general.

Paired Smoother: An example is the Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother, which is specifically paired with the Kalman filter.
Complex Smoothers: For particle filters, smoothing and resampling schemes can be more complicated and may require filter-specific implementations.



Ancillary Tools for Performance
To ensure high performance, especially for complex schemes, the library should incorporate specialized data structures and algorithms.

Example: For particle filters operating on spatial data, a k-d tree could be implemented to accelerate the lookup and resampling of large particle fields based on their location.

The overall goal is to design interfaces that are modular enough to accommodate these major structural variations as new algorithms and techniques are implemented.

title: Python Integration
text: This guide details the internal architecture of Neuralyzer’s Python integration, explaining how the embedded interpreter works, how data is marshaled between C++ and Python, and how to extend the bindings.

title: Python Integration
text:
Architecture Overview
The Python integration is built on three main components:

PythonWidget (Qt UI):

Located in src/WhiskerToolbox/Python_Widget.
Handles the visual interface: Console, Editor, and Properties panel.
Manages the PythonEngine instance.
Connects UI signals (like “Run” button) to the engine’s execute() method.

PythonEngine (Embedded Interpreter):

Located in src/python_bindings/PythonEngine.cpp.
Wraps pybind11::embed.
Manages the Python interpreter lifecycle (initialization, finalization).
Maintains the globals() dictionary to persist state across executions (REPL behavior).
Redirects sys.stdout and sys.stderr to C++ callbacks for display in the UI.

PythonBridge (Data Marshalling):

Located in src/python_bindings/PythonBridge.cpp.
Acts as the bridge between the application’s DataManager and the Python environment.
Injects the dm proxy object into the Python namespace on startup.
Handles the conversion of C++ data types to Python objects and vice-versa.

title: Python Integration
text:
Bindings (whiskertoolbox_python)
The core of the integration is the whiskertoolbox_python PyBind11 module. This module exposes C++ classes to Python. It is embedded directly into the application binary, so there is no separate .pyd or .so file to deploy.
Source location: src/python_bindings/

Key Binding Files

bind_module.hpp: Forward declarations for binding functions.
bindings.cpp: The main PYBIND11_EMBEDDED_MODULE definition. Calls individual init functions.
numpy_utils.hpp: Helper functions for zero-copy NumPy array creation.
bind_datamanager.cpp: Binds the DataManager class and its methods.
bind_analog.cpp: Binds AnalogTimeSeries.
bind_point.cpp: Binds PointData and Point2D.
bind_tensor.cpp: Binds TensorData.

title: Python Integration
text:
Data Types and Zero-Copy Strategy
To ensure high performance with large datasets (e.g., electrophysiology or high-speed video data), we prioritize zero-copy access where possible.

AnalogTimeSeries & TensorData
These types store data in contiguous memory blocks (std::vector or similar). We expose these buffers to Python as read-only NumPy arrays.

C++ Side: std::span<float const>
Python Side: numpy.ndarray (flags: WRITEABLE=False)

This allows users to use libraries like numpy and scipy directly on the data without the overhead of copying millions of samples.


Ragged Data (Points, Lines, Masks)
Data types that are “ragged” (variable number of elements per time point) are more difficult to map directly to NumPy. * Currently, these are exposed via std::vector copies (e.g., getAtTime(t) returns a list of objects). * Future optimization may involve creating custom iterators or structured NumPy arrays.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text: PlottingSVG is a static library that converts CorePlotting::RenderableScene objects into publication-quality SVG documents. It is the SVG counterpart to PlottingOpenGL — both consume the same CorePlotting scene graph but produce different output: OpenGL draw calls vs. SVG strings.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text: PlottingSVG is a static library that converts CorePlotting::RenderableScene objects into publication-quality SVG documents. It is the SVG counterpart to PlottingOpenGL — both consume the same CorePlotting scene graph but produce different output: OpenGL draw calls vs. SVG strings.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text:
Key Features

Symmetric with PlottingOpenGL: Same input (RenderableScene), different output. Any widget that builds a RenderableScene can export to SVG with no additional scene-building code.
No Qt Dependency: Pure C++ string output using <sstream> and <fstream>. Can be used in headless/batch workflows without a GUI.
Decoration System: Extensible overlay mechanism for axes, scalebars, center lines, and other SVG-specific annotations that have no OpenGL equivalent.
Per-Batch Renderers: Dedicated renderer classes for each primitive type (polylines, glyphs, rectangles), matching the PlottingOpenGL renderer organization.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text:
Motivation
Prior to this library, SVG export logic lived inside CorePlotting/Export/SVGPrimitives (now removed). DataViewer_Widget/Rendering/SVGExporter still builds a RenderableScene from DataViewer-specific state, but links PlottingSVG and calls PlottingSVG::buildSVGDocument() / createScalebarSVG().
This arrangement had two problems:

Architectural asymmetry: OpenGL rendering lives in its own library (PlottingOpenGL), but SVG rendering was embedded in CorePlotting. CorePlotting should contain no rendering backend code.
No reuse path: Each new widget that wanted SVG export would need its own bespoke exporter class, duplicating the scene-to-SVG conversion and document assembly logic.

PlottingSVG fixes both issues by extracting SVG rendering into a proper library that any widget can consume.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text:
Architecture

Position in the Stack
CorePlotting (data types, layout, scene building)
    ├── PlottingOpenGL  (RenderableScene → OpenGL draw calls)
    └── PlottingSVG     (RenderableScene → SVG strings)
Both rendering backends depend on CorePlotting but not on each other. Widget code depends on PlottingOpenGL for live rendering and optionally on PlottingSVG for export.

title: PlottingSVG Library
PlottingSVG Library
PlottingSVG Library
text:
Rendering Pipeline
The internal rendering flow mirrors PlottingOpenGL’s approach:
SVGSceneRenderer::render()
    │
    ├── SVGDocument::setBackground()
    │
    ├── For each batch type (in render order):
    │   ├── SVGRectangleRenderer::render(batch, V, P, canvas) → elements
    │   ├── SVGPolyLineRenderer::render(batch, V, P, canvas) → elements
    │   └── SVGGlyphRenderer::render(batch, V, P, canvas) → elements
    │
    ├── For each decoration:
    │   └── decoration->render(canvas_width, canvas_height) → elements
    │
    └── SVGDocument::build() → complete SVG string

Coordinate Transform
Each per-batch renderer computes MVP = Projection × View × Model and transforms world-space vertices to SVG pixel coordinates:

Apply MVP: ndc = MVP * vertex
Perspective divide: ndc /= ndc.w
Map NDC → SVG: svg_x = width * (ndc.x + 1) / 2, svg_y = height * (1 - ndc.y) / 2

This is identical to the transform in PlottingSVG::transformVertexToSVG() (re-exported as CorePlotting::transformVertexToSVG() for legacy callers), ensuring pixel-perfect correspondence between OpenGL and SVG output.

Tests reside in tests/PlottingSVG/ and verify:







Test Category
What It Verifies




Coordinate transform
transformVertexToSVG() produces correct SVG pixel positions for known MVP inputs


Color conversion
colorToSVGHex() handles edge cases (0, 1, out-of-range clamping)


Glyph rendering
Each glyph type (Tick, Circle, Square, Cross) produces correct SVG elements


PolyLine rendering
Multi-segment lines with per-line colors produce correct <polyline> elements


Rectangle rendering
Rectangles with alpha produce correct <rect> elements with fill-opacity


Scene rendering
Full scene with mixed batch types produces elements in correct layer order


Document structure
Output contains valid XML header, viewBox, background rect, closing tag


Decoration rendering
Scalebar and axis decorations produce positioned elements in canvas coordinates


Round-trip consistency
Same RenderableScene produces same SVG output across multiple render() calls



Tests use Catch2 and do not require an OpenGL context or Qt event loop.

Create src/PlotDataExport/RasterCSVExport.hpp.
Structs:
struct RasterSeriesInput {
    std::string event_key;
    GatherResult<DigitalEventSeries> const& gathered;
    TimeFrame const* time_frame;
};

struct RasterExportMetadata {
    std::string alignment_key;
    double window_size = 0.0;
};
Functions:
[[nodiscard]] std::string exportRasterToCSV(
    std::vector<RasterSeriesInput> const& series,
    RasterExportMetadata const& metadata = {},
    std::string_view delimiter = ",");
Algorithm: 1. Write metadata comment header (# export_type: raster, # alignment_key: ..., etc.). 2. Write CSV header: trial_index<delim>event_key<delim>relative_time. 3. For each series → for each trial → for each event in trial view: - int64_t alignment = gathered.alignmentTimeAt(trial_idx) - int64_t abs_time = time_frame->getTimeAtIndex(event.time()) - double relative = static_cast<double>(abs_time - alignment) - Append row: trial_idx<delim>event_key<delim>relative.

Algorithm (aggregate): 1. Write metadata comment header. 2. Compute bin centers from the first row: bin_start + (i + 0.5) * bin_width. 3. Write header: unit_key<delim><center_0><delim><center_1><delim>.... 4. For each unit i: write unit_keys[i]<delim>rows[i].values[0]<delim>....
Algorithm (per-trial): 1. Write metadata comment header. 2. Write header: unit_key<delim>trial_index<delim>bin_center<delim>value. 3. For each unit → for each trial → for each time bin: - Append row from rate_data[unit].trials.per_trial_values[trial][bin].

Implementation note: The per-trial function takes vector<PerTrialHeatmapInput> rather than vector<RateEstimateWithTrials> directly. EventRateEstimation lives under the UI layer (gated by ENABLE_UI) so adding it as a dependency of PlotDataExport would break non-UI builds and tests. Widgets convert RateEstimateWithTrials → PerTrialHeatmapInput before calling the export API.

title: ParameterSchema Library
text:
ParameterSchema is a lightweight, non-Qt static library at src/ParameterSchema/ that provides compile-time parameter schema extraction for reflect-cpp structs. It is a shared dependency used by both TransformsV2 (for transform parameter forms) and the Command Architecture (for command introspection and guided pipeline editors).
The library has no Qt dependency and depends only on reflect-cpp and the C++ standard library.

Key Types

ParameterFieldDescriptor
Describes a single field in a parameter struct at runtime:








Field
Type
Description

Reflect-cpp field name (snake_case)

std::string
Underlying type: "float", "int", "std::string", "bool", "enum"

std::string
Full raw type string from reflect-cpp


display_name
std::string
Human-readable “Title Case” label


min_value / max_value
std::optional<double>
From rfl::Validator constraints


is_exclusive_min/max
bool
Exclusive vs. inclusive bound


allowed_values
std::vector<std::string>
For enum-like string fields; auto-populated for enum class fields


default_value_json
std::optional<std::string>
Default value as JSON string


tooltip
std::string
UI hint (from ParameterUIHints)


group
std::string
Grouping label for the UI


is_advanced
bool
Collapsed by default in the UI


is_optional
bool
True for std::optional<T> fields


is_bound
bool
True if typically populated from a value store


dynamic_combo
bool
If true, create QComboBox even with empty allowed_values


include_none_sentinel
bool
If true, prepend “(None)” sentinel to combo (maps to "" in JSON)


is_variant
bool
True for rfl::TaggedUnion fields


variant_discriminator
std::string
Tag field name (e.g. "model")


variant_alternatives
std::vector<VariantAlternative>
One entry per union alternative





ParameterSchema
Holds the complete schema for one parameter struct:
struct ParameterSchema {
    std::string params_type_name;
    std::vector<ParameterFieldDescriptor> fields;

    ParameterFieldDescriptor * field(std::string const & name);
    ParameterFieldDescriptor const * field(std::string const & name) const;
};


ParameterUIHints<T>
A template trait struct for providing custom UI annotations. Specialize it alongside a params struct to add tooltips, allowed values, grouping, and ordering without modifying the struct itself:
template<>
struct ParameterUIHints<MyParams> {
    static void annotate(ParameterSchema & schema) {
        schema.field("threshold")->tooltip = "Detection threshold (0.0–1.0)";
        schema.field("mode")->allowed_values = {"Fast", "Accurate"};
    }
};

Observer Library
text:
Usage in WhiskerToolbox
The Observer library is fundamental to WhiskerToolbox’s reactive architecture:

DataManager: All data types (PointData, LineData, MaskData, etc.) use observers to notify the UI when data changes
Transforms: Output data objects observe their input sources to automatically recalculate when inputs change
TableView: Tables observe their source data and row/column selectors to update when dependencies change
UI Widgets: Qt widgets register observers on data objects to refresh their display

┌─────────────┐     notifies     ┌─────────────┐     notifies     ┌─────────────┐
│  Raw Data   │ ───────────────► │  Transform  │ ───────────────► │  UI Widget  │

└─────────────┘                  └─────────────┘                  └─────────────┘

title: Observer Library
text:
Important Limitations






WarningNot Thread-Safe



The Observer library is not thread-safe. All operations (addObserver, removeObserver, notifyObservers) must be called from the same thread, or external synchronization must be provided.








WarningNo Modification During Notification



Adding or removing observers from within an observer callback during notifyObservers() results in undefined behavior. If you need to modify observers in response to a notification, defer the modification until after the notification completes.








NoteException Behavior



If an observer callback throws an exception, remaining observers will not be notified. The exception propagates to the caller of notifyObservers(). Design callbacks to be exception-safe.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
The classification pipeline implements ground-truth (GT) substitution: after Viterbi decoding, predictions for labeled frames are overwritten with their known labels. This ensures the final output is exact on training data, but it means train-set metrics are always 100% — which is useless for evaluation.
Additionally, the existing “validation” heuristic (frames outside the training region) is unreliable because many non-training frames have no labels at all, and unlabeled frames do not represent class 0.
Two features address this:

Explicit validation intervals — a dedicated DigitalIntervalSeries specifying regions with known labels for honest evaluation.
Leave-one-interval-out cross-validation — retrain the model multiple times, each time holding out one training interval, predict it with boundary constraints, and average per-fold metrics.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
The classification pipeline implements ground-truth (GT) substitution: after Viterbi decoding, predictions for labeled frames are overwritten with their known labels. This ensures the final output is exact on training data, but it means train-set metrics are always 100% — which is useless for evaluation.
Additionally, the existing “validation” heuristic (frames outside the training region) is unreliable because many non-training frames have no labels at all, and unlabeled frames do not represent class 0.
Two features address this:

Explicit validation intervals — a dedicated DigitalIntervalSeries specifying regions with known labels for honest evaluation.
Leave-one-interval-out cross-validation — retrain the model multiple times, each time holding out one training interval, predict it with boundary constraints, and average per-fold metrics.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
Architecture

Raw vs. GT-Substituted Predictions
The pipeline maintains two prediction vectors:

raw_predictions — the model’s actual Viterbi output, unmodified. Used for all metric computations.
predictions — after GT substitution (training frame labels overwrite model output). Used only for the final output writer (PredictionWriter), so downstream consumers get clean labeled data.

This split ensures metrics reflect true model performance while the output retains exact labels on known frames.


Validation Intervals
Config field: validation_interval_key (std::string)
When set, the pipeline partitions predicted frames into three buckets:








Bucket
Source
Metrics computed?




Training
Frames inside training_interval_key
Yes (train)


Validation
Frames inside validation_interval_key
Yes (validation)


Other
All remaining frames
No



Ground-truth labels for validation frames are assembled using the same label configuration as training (e.g., LabelFromIntervals with the same contact interval series). The key difference is that validation intervals are not used for training — the model has never seen these labels.
Validation intervals still benefit from boundary-constrained decoding: the first and last frames of a validation interval (which have known labels) serve as Viterbi bookends, just like training interval boundaries.


Leave-One-Interval-Out Cross-Validation
Config field: max_cv_folds (std::size_t, default 5; 0 = disabled)
Cross-validation runs as Stage 5c, after the main model is trained in Stage 5b. It does not affect the main model or its predictions — it is purely an evaluation mechanism.

Algorithm
For \(K\) training intervals (capped at max_cv_folds):

Hold out interval \(k\) from the training set.
Retrain a fresh model on the remaining \(K-1\) intervals.
Predict the held-out interval using the retrained model:

Segment the held-out interval’s features into contiguous sequences.
Apply bidirectional boundary constraints: the first and last frames of the held-out interval have known labels (from the full label assembly), which serve as initial and terminal Viterbi constraints.
Run predictSequencesBidirectionalConstrained().

Compute per-fold metrics by comparing raw predictions to ground truth on the held-out interval.
Average metrics across all \(K\) folds.

The main model (trained on ALL intervals) remains the one used for Stage 6 prediction. CV results are stored in separate result fields.


Why Full Retrain?
Each fold retrains from scratch rather than using the main model. This is because the HMM’s transition matrix, emission distributions, and initial state distribution are all estimated from training data. Removing one interval changes these parameters, and the difference is the signal we want to measure — how much does the model depend on each block of labeled data?


Boundary Constraints in CV
The held-out interval’s own first and last frame labels serve as bookends. These labels come from the label assembly (which covers all labeled frames), not from the training label_map (which excludes the held-out interval). This is realistic: in production, adjacent labeled blocks provide boundary constraints for unlabeled gaps between them.

text:

TensorData: "features" (100,000 frames × 192 features)
Labels: "contact" DigitalIntervalSeries (contact events)

Validation region: "validate" DIS with intervals [3000–4000], [7000–7500]

CV holds out each training interval in turn (3 folds), retrains on the other 2, predicts the held-out interval with boundary constraints, and reports per-fold accuracy.
Main model predicts all 100k frames. Viterbi uses boundary constraints at labeled block boundaries.
Train metrics: raw predictions vs ground truth on training-region frames.
Validation metrics: raw predictions vs ground truth on validation-region frames.
Output: GT-substituted predictions + probabilities written to DataManager.

title: Supervised PCA Operation
text:
SupervisedPCAOperation is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that fits PCA exclusively on the labeled subset of observations. The principal components therefore capture variance within the labeled data, not the entire dataset. All observations (labeled and unlabeled) are then projected into the resulting space.
This is useful when the labeled data represents a specific phenomenon of interest (e.g., whisker contact frames), and the user wants the top principal components to reflect variance within that phenomenon rather than variance across the full recording.

title: Supervised PCA Operation
text:
Architecture

Class Hierarchy
MLModelOperation (interface)
  └── MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (abstract base)
        ├── LogitProjectionOperation
        └── SupervisedPCAOperation (this class)


Pimpl Pattern
The implementation uses the pimpl idiom to keep Armadillo matrix members out of the header:
SupervisedPCAOperation.hpp  →  MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (public API)
SupervisedPCAOperation.cpp  →  eigenvectors, eigenvalues, mean, stddev (hidden)
The Impl struct holds:

eigenvectors — \((D \times n\_components)\) projection matrix
eigenvalues — sorted descending
mean — per-feature mean (from labeled subset)
total_variance — sum of all eigenvalues (for variance ratio computation)

title: Supervised PCA Operation
text:
Algorithm

fitTransform

Validate inputs (non-empty, matching dimensions, ≥ 2 classes, n_components ≤ D)
Compute statistics from labeled subset: per-feature mean
Center labeled data (subtract mean)
Covariance matrix from centered labeled data: \(\Sigma = \frac{1}{N-1} X_c X_c^T\)
Eigendecomposition via arma::eig_sym, reversed to descending order
Truncate to top n_components eigenvectors
Project ALL data (not just labeled) using the fitted eigenvectors and mean



transform
Uses the stored eigenvectors and mean to project new data without retraining.

text:
The SequenceAssembler (pipelines/SequenceAssembler.hpp) segments a flat feature matrix and associated time indices into contiguous temporal sequences. This is essential for sequence models like HMMs that require observations grouped into runs of consecutive time steps.
TensorData may have gaps in its TimeFrameIndex rows (e.g., frames 100–200 then 500–600). The SequenceAssembler detects these gaps and splits the flat matrix into separate SequenceSegment objects, one per contiguous run.

title: Sequence Assembler
text:
Gap Detection
A gap occurs when consecutive TimeFrameIndex values differ by more than 1:
times[i+1] - times[i] > 1  →  new sequence starts at i+1
For example, given times {0, 1, 2, 10, 11, 12}:

Run 1: indices 0–2 (times 0, 1, 2)
Run 2: indices 3–5 (times 10, 11, 12)

Models that implement trainSequences() / predictSequences() (e.g., HMM) receive the segmented sequences directly. Frame-based models skip the segmentation stage entirely.

title: Logit Projection Operation
text:
LogitProjectionOperation is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that trains a softmax regression classifier on labeled feature data and extracts the raw pre-softmax logit activations as a discriminative \(C\)-dimensional projection. The output is a \((C \times N)\) matrix where each column holds the class logit scores for one observation.
Since logits represent the linear decision boundary in feature space, this is equivalent to a supervised linear projection — a data-driven counterpart to PCA that maximizes class separation rather than variance.

title: Logit Projection Operation
text:
Architecture

Class Hierarchy
MLModelOperation (interface)
  └── MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (abstract base)
        └── LogitProjectionOperation (concrete)
MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation parallels MLDimReductionOperation for unsupervised reduction. It adds a labeled fitTransform() method while routing train() to fitTransform() (discarding the output) so the operation is compatible with the standard registry workflow.


Pimpl Pattern
The implementation uses the pimpl idiom to isolate mlpack.hpp from consumers:
LogitProjectionOperation.hpp  →  MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (public API)
LogitProjectionOperation.cpp  →  mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat> (hidden)
The Impl struct holds:

std::unique_ptr<mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat>> — the trained model (used only during fitTransform)
arma::mat weight_matrix — extracted weight matrix \(W\) of shape \((C \times D)\)
arma::vec bias — extracted bias vector \(b\) of shape \((C)\)
num_classes, num_features, col_names — metadata
trained — readiness flag

After fitTransform(), the mlpack model is retained in memory. After load(), the model pointer is null — transform() works without mlpack in both cases because it uses the extracted \(W\) and \(b\) directly.


Training and Weight Extraction
Training uses fitIntercept=true for better model expressiveness:
ens::L_BFGS optimizer;
optimizer.MaxIterations() = max_iterations;

model = std::make_unique<SRModel>(
    features, labels, num_classes, optimizer, lambda, true);  // fitIntercept=true
With fitIntercept=true, Parameters() returns a \((C \times (D+1))\) matrix:

Column 0: bias vector
Columns 1..D: weight matrix

Extraction:
bias = model->Parameters().col(0);           // (C,)
weight_matrix = model->Parameters().cols(1, D);  // (C, D)


Logit Computation
The forward pass for new data \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times N}\):
result = weight_matrix * features;   // (C, N)
result.each_col() += bias;           // broadcast add bias


Serialization
Save/load stores only \(W\) and \(b\) (not the mlpack model), using cereal::BinaryOutputArchive:
[num_classes][num_features][col_names][weight_matrix][bias]
This makes the serialized artifact self-contained for inference without mlpack dependencies.

title: MLCore Library
text:
Key Design Decisions

TensorData as Feature Matrix
Feature assembly is not part of MLCore. Users build feature tensors using the TensorDesigner/TensorColumnBuilders infrastructure. MLCore validates, converts (float→double, NaN handling, z-score normalization), and consumes the result via FeatureConverter.


Pimpl Pattern for Model Isolation
All model operations (Random Forest, K-Means, etc.) use the pimpl idiom to isolate mlpack headers from consumers. This keeps compile times reasonable and prevents mlpack’s transitive includes from leaking.


Putative Group Output Pattern
Predictions never overwrite user labels. Output goes to groups prefixed with the configured prefix (e.g., "Predicted:Contact", "Cluster:0"). This follows the pattern established by LineKalmanGrouping elsewhere in the project.


Three Label Modes
Labels can come from:

DigitalIntervalSeries — binary labeling (inside=positive, outside=negative)
TimeEntity groups — multi-class from entity group membership at each frame
Data-entity groups — multi-class from data object group membership

See Label Assembly for details.

text:
HiddenMarkovModelOperation wraps mlpack::HMM<Distribution> to provide sequence-aware classification within the MLCore framework. Emission Type Selection
The use_diagonal_covariance and use_gmm_emissions flags combine orthogonally:



use_gmm_emissions

GMM Emissions
When use_gmm_emissions is true, each hidden state uses an mlpack::GMM (or mlpack::DiagonalGMM) as its emission distribution instead of a single Gaussian. This allows each state to model multi-modal observation distributions 014 useful when a single hidden state actually encompasses multiple sub-states with distinct emission characteristics.
Each state019s GMM has num_gaussians components. During supervised training, mlpack fits the mixture via EM on the observations assigned to that state. Prediction (Viterbi, Forward-Backward) works identically to the single-Gaussian case; only the emission probability computation changes.
The isGMMEmissions() and numGaussiansPerState() methods report the active configuration after training. Serialization includes the GMM flag and component count, so loaded models correctly reconstruct the matching HMM variant.


Diagonal Covariance
When use_diagonal_covariance is true, the HMM uses mlpack::DiagonalGaussianDistribution<> instead of full covariance. This:

Reduces covariance parameters per state from \(\frac{M(M+1)}{2}\) to \(M\)
Reduces emission evaluation cost from \(O(M^2)\) to \(O(M)\)
Improves numerical stability with limited training data
Assumes features are conditionally independent given the hidden state

The isDiagonalCovariance() method reports the active variant after training. Serialization includes the diagonal flag, so loaded models correctly reconstruct the matching HMM type.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian / GMM)
text:
Limitations

Supervised only: The current implementation requires labeled sequences. Unsupervised Baum-Welch training (EM) is not exposed, though mlpack supports it.
Gaussian / GMM emissions: Four emission variants are supported (full/diagonal Gaussian, full/diagonal GMM). Discrete emissions are not supported.
Fixed state count: The number of states must be specified before training. Model selection (choosing the optimal state count) must be done manually.
No warm-starting: Each train() / trainSequences() call initializes a fresh HMM. Incremental refinement of an existing model is not supported.
Memory: The Forward-Backward algorithm allocates a (num_states × observations) probability matrix. Very long sequences with many states may consume significant memory.

title: Media_Widget Refactoring Roadmap
text:
Media_Widget was the first visualization widget in WhiskerToolbox. It is built on a QGraphicsScene backend (Media_Window) with bespoke rendering, interaction, and configuration code for every data type it displays (media, lines, points, masks, tensors, intervals). Since its creation, the project has developed a mature, modular plotting stack:

CorePlotting — API-agnostic mappers, scene graph, hit testing, interaction controllers
PlottingOpenGL — GPU-accelerated batch renderers (glyphs, polylines, rectangles)
Plots/Common — Reusable Qt widgets (GlyphStyleControls, LineStyleControls, ColormapControls, PlotTooltipManager, axis widgets, PlotInteractionHelpers)
AutoParamWidget — Schema-driven auto-generated parameter forms
ParameterSchema — Compile-time schema extraction from reflect-cpp structs

Media_Widget duplicates significant portions of this infrastructure. Adding new features is difficult because the rendering pipeline, interaction handling, and UI controls are tightly coupled.


The motivating feature — plotting data (masks, lines, points) when no media is loaded — is blocked not by a hard technical limitation, but by entanglement. The canvas size is already independent of media resolution (driven by QGraphicsView widget size), and _clearMedia() just fills black. The real issues are:

The _plotMediaData() method has interleaved concerns: media rendering, transparency mask application, colormap processing, and multi-media compositing
The overlay rendering methods (_plotLineData, _plotMaskData, etc.) use aspect-ratio scaling factors derived from media dimensions for coordinate conversion
There’s no explicit “canvas-only mode” — the widget treats media absence as “nothing to show” rather than “show overlays on blank canvas”








These can be done independently, in any order, without touching the rendering pipeline.


Status: ✅ Complete
Replaced bespoke ColorPicker_Widget, point size slider/spinbox, and marker shape combo box with an embedded GlyphStyleControls + GlyphStyleState instance. PointMarkerShape enum was removed; PointDisplayOptions::marker_shape now uses CorePlotting::GlyphType directly. The rendering code in Media_Window::_plotPointData() was updated to switch on CorePlotting::GlyphType values. The Tick glyph type (vertical line) replaces the old X marker shape.



Status: ✅ Complete
Replaced bespoke ColorPicker_Widget, line thickness slider/spinbox with an embedded LineStyleControls + LineStyleState instance. The color, alpha, and thickness controls are now provided by the reusable LineStyleControls widget from Plots/Common/LineStyleControls/. Line-specific controls (show_points, edge_snapping, segment controls, position_marker) remain unchanged as domain-specific features.



What exists: - Bespoke color picker and alpha slider (same pattern as points/lines) - Mask-specific toggles: show_bounding_box, show_outline, use_as_transparency
Approach: - For color + alpha: embed LineStyleControls (it provides color + alpha, thickness can be hidden/ignored) or create a simpler ColorAlphaControls widget if that feels cleaner - The mask-specific checkboxes remain as-is



What exists (5 bespoke selection widgets):







Widget
Parameters

Good candidates: LineAddSelectionWidget, LineEraseSelectionWidget, LineSelectSelectionWidget
These have simple scalar/bool/enum parameters that map directly to ParameterSchema + AutoParamWidget. The same pattern already works for media processing options.
Not a good candidate: LineDrawAllFramesSelectionWidget has a stateful workflow (start drawing → accumulate points → complete → apply). This is genuinely interactive, not just parameter configuration.
Approach: 1. Define reflect-cpp structs for each (e.g., LineAddParams, LineEraseParams, LineSelectParams) 2. Replace each widget body with AutoParamWidget + connect parametersChanged() to the existing signal emissions
Estimated scope per widget: ~40-60 lines removed, ~20 lines added

These changes address the immediate pain point of rendering without media.


Current state:
The coordinate mapping has three interacting pieces:

Canvas pixel dimensions (_canvasWidth, _canvasHeight): fixed at 640×480 by default. This is the QGraphicsScene / QImage backing size. Media frames are scaled to this size.
Canvas coordinate system: the logical resolution that overlay data coordinates are interpreted against. Currently this is implicitly the active media’s native resolution (e.g., 640×480 for a 640×480 video). getXAspect() = _canvasWidth / media.getWidth() and getYAspect() = _canvasHeight / media.getHeight().
Per-data ImageSize: LineData, PointData, and MaskData each carry an ImageSize (from RaggedTimeSeries). If defined (not -1,‑1), the overlay rendering substitutes this for the media resolution, computing xAspect = _canvasWidth / data.getImageSize().width. If undefined (-1,‑1), the data trusts the media resolution.

Key behaviors to preserve (and formalize):

MediaData is always “correct”: its native resolution defines the authoritative canvas coordinate system when loaded. (Note: MediaData defaults to 640×480 when uninitialized — it never uses -1,‑1 — so an empty media object silently produces a coordinate system that may not match loaded overlay data.)
ImageSize -1,‑1 means “undefined”: data objects with undefined image size defer to the canvas coordinate system (currently media).
Scaling is “stretch to fill”, not “spatial subset”: when PointData has ImageSize 256×256 and media is 640×480, the points are scaled up so the 256×256 grid fills the full canvas. The implicit assumption is that the lower-resolution data represents the same spatial extent at coarser sampling, not a 256×256 crop of the 640×480 field of view. There is currently no way to express the alternative interpretation.

Problems this creates for no-media mode:

The program launches with empty MediaData whose size defaults to 640×480. If overlay data (e.g., masks at 512×512) is loaded without media, getXAspect() returns 1.0 (because no visible media → fallback), which silently misaligns data that expects coordinate mapping.
There is no explicit “canvas coordinate system” object — it is scattered across getXAspect(), getYAspect(), and per-overlay ad-hoc scaling logic, making it impossible for the user to inspect or override.
There is no mechanism for a data object to declare whether it should be stretched to fill the canvas or whether it represents a spatial subset (crop / ROI) of the canvas coordinates.

Approach:

Introduce CanvasCoordinateSystem — a small struct holding the logical { width, height } that defines the coordinate space overlays are plotted into. This replaces the implicit “ask the active media for its resolution” pattern.
Resolution priority chain — the canvas coordinate system should be determined by the first source that provides a valid (non -1,‑1) resolution, in this order:

User override (explicit manual setting via UI / state — highest priority)
Active media (MediaData::getImageSize(), if visible and not default-only)
First loaded data object with defined ImageSize (e.g., a MaskData at 512×512)
Fallback default (640×480, matching the current behavior)

When media is loaded/unloaded or data objects are added/removed, the coordinate system should be re-evaluated unless there is an active user override.
Per-data coordinate mapping mode — add a per-data-object setting (likely in the display options, e.g., PointDisplayOptions, LineDisplayOptions, MaskDisplayOptions) that controls how the data’s ImageSize relates to the canvas:








Mode
Meaning
Scaling




ScaleToCanvas (default)
Data covers the full canvas extent at its own resolution. Equivalent to current behavior.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / data.imageSize.width


SubsetOfCanvas
Data occupies a spatial sub-region. Coordinates are in canvas-coordinate-system units already.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / canvasCoordSystem.width (same as media-based scaling)



ScaleToCanvas preserves backward compatibility: data at 256×256 is stretched to fill a 640×480 canvas. SubsetOfCanvas allows, e.g., a 256×256 point cloud that lives in the top-left quadrant of a 640×480 canvas.
When ImageSize is -1,‑1, the mode is moot — the data uses the canvas coordinate system directly (equivalent to SubsetOfCanvas with matching dimensions).
Replace getXAspect() / getYAspect() — these methods currently encode the full priority chain in an ad-hoc way. Replace them with a single method (or free function) that takes CanvasCoordinateSystem, the data’s ImageSize, and the mapping mode, returning the x/y scale factors. All _plotXxxData() methods call this instead of computing their own scaling.
UI for canvas coordinate system — expose the resolved canvas coordinate system in the Media_Widget UI (read-only display showing source: “from media”, “from MaskData ‘whiskers’”, “manual override”). Provide width/height spinboxes for manual override. This can live in MediaWidgetState as a serializable field.

Status: ✅ Complete
Sub-tasks: - [x] Define CanvasCoordinateSystem struct — src/CorePlotting/Layout/CanvasCoordinateSystem.hpp - [x] Define CoordinateMappingMode enum (ScaleToCanvas, SubsetOfCanvas) — same file - [x] Add CoordinateMappingMode field to LineDisplayOptions, PointDisplayOptions, MaskDisplayOptions (default: ScaleToCanvas) — DisplayOptions.hpp - [x] Add CanvasCoordinateSystem to MediaWidgetState (with optional user override) — MediaWidgetStateData.hpp, MediaWidgetState.hpp/.cpp - [x] Implement resolution priority chain in Media_Window::resolveCanvasCoordinateSystem() — called at the top of each UpdateCanvas(); priority: user override → active media → first data object with defined ImageSize → 640×480 fallback - [x] Replace getXAspect() / getYAspect() with unified scaling function — computeScalingFactors() / computeInverseScalingFactors() free functions in CanvasCoordinateSystem.hpp; getXAspect()/getYAspect() kept as backward-compatible wrappers (used by MediaLine_Widget.cpp) - [x] Update all _plotXxxData() and hit-testing methods to use new scaling function — _plotLineData, _plotPointData, _plotMaskData (bounding box), _findLineAtPosition, _findPointAtPosition (bug fix: was ignoring ImageSize entirely), _findMaskAtPosition, updateTemporaryLine (bug fix: fetched ImageSize but never used it) - [x] Add UI controls in Media_Widget for viewing/overriding canvas coordinate system — CanvasCoord_Widget in Media_Widget/UI/, integrated into MediaPropertiesWidget as a collapsible section; shows resolved width×height and source, with manual override via QCheckBox + QSpinBox pair - [x] Unit tests for coordinate mapping (pure math, no Qt dependency) — tests/CorePlotting/CanvasCoordinateSystem.test.cpp, 19 test cases / 44 assertions
This is the key unlock — once the canvas coordinate system is an explicit, inspectable, overridable entity, overlay rendering becomes independent of media presence, and plotting without media becomes trivial.



Completed prerequisite: Media_Widget::setDataManager() now calls updateMedia() at the end of setup, wiring the QGraphicsScene to the QGraphicsView immediately on widget creation. Previously this was only called from MainWindow::loadData(), which meant overlays were invisible until the user loaded a media file. The legacy loop in MainWindow::loadData() has been removed.
Remaining approach: 1. Add a bool _has_media flag or derive from whether any media data key is registered 2. In UpdateCanvas(): if no media, skip _plotMediaData() but still render all overlays 3. Allow background color configuration (currently hardcoded black) 4. Support user-specified canvas dimensions via state when no media is loaded
Estimated scope: ~50 lines — mostly guard changes in UpdateCanvas() and _plotMediaData(), plus a state field for “background_color”



Current state: - getXAspect(), getYAspect(), _getMediaScaledPosition() are methods on Media_Window - Each overlay type has its own scaling logic scattered through 1800+ lines of Media_Window.cpp
Approach: 1. Create a free-function utility: CanvasPoint mapToCanvas(DataPoint, CanvasCoordinateSystem, DataBounds) 2. Use it in all _plotXxxData() methods 3. This also makes it testable without Qt (unit tests for coordinate math)





These integrate Media_Widget’s rendering with the modern stack.


Current state: - _plotLineData() manually iterates LineData, creates QPainterPath, scales coordinates - _plotPointData() manually creates QGraphicsItems per marker shape - _plotMaskData() manually iterates Mask2D pixels, creates QImages
CorePlotting already has: - SpatialMapper::mapPointsAtTime() → MappedElement (position + entity_id) - SpatialMapper::mapLinesAtTime() → MappedLineView (vertices + entity_id) - MaskContourMapper::mapMaskContoursAtTime() → OwningLineView (boundary polylines) - HeatmapMapper::toRectangleBatch() → colored rectangles
Approach: 1. Replace the data traversal in each _plotXxxData() with CorePlotting mapper calls 2. Convert mapper output → QGraphicsItems (not OpenGL — we’re staying on QGraphicsScene for now) 3. This decouples data interpretation from rendering and gives us entity tracking for free
Value: Immediate bugfix potential — the mappers handle cross-TimeFrame queries correctly, which the bespoke code may not. Also enables hit testing via SceneHitTester.



Current state: - _findLineAtPosition() — manual perpendicular distance calculation - _findPointAtPosition() — manual Euclidean distance - _findMaskAtPosition() — manual pixel membership check - Each is a separate method with hardcoded thresholds
CorePlotting already has: - SceneHitTester — multi-strategy hit testing (QuadTree for discrete elements, containment for rectangles/masks) - Returns HitTestResult with entity_id and hit priority
Approach: 1. After mapping data with CorePlotting mappers (3.1), build a RenderableScene with spatial index 2. Replace _findXxxAtPosition() methods with SceneHitTester::hitTest() 3. Unifies all selection to one code path



Current state: - Media_Window handles mouse events directly with mode-specific behavior - Drawing modes accumulate _drawing_points - Hover circle is manually managed
CorePlotting already has: - LineInteractionController — free-form line drawing tool - IGlyphInteractionController — brush/circle tools - GlyphPreview — visual feedback for tools (hover circles, selection highlights)
Approach: 1. Create thin adapter between Media_Window mouse events and CorePlotting interaction controllers 2. This may not be worth doing unless Media_Widget moves to the OpenGL stack (Tier 4)





These are larger refactors that would fully modernize Media_Widget.


Rationale: - PlottingOpenGL implements CorePlotting’s RenderableScene → GPU rendering - A PlottingQt library would implement the same → QGraphicsScene rendering - This would let Media_Widget use CorePlotting’s full pipeline without switching to OpenGL

title: Media_Widget Refactoring Roadmap
text:
Media_Widget was the first visualization widget in WhiskerToolbox. It is built on a QGraphicsScene backend (Media_Window) with bespoke rendering, interaction, and configuration code for every data type it displays (media, lines, points, masks, tensors, intervals). Since its creation, the project has developed a mature, modular plotting stack:

CorePlotting — API-agnostic mappers, scene graph, hit testing, interaction controllers
PlottingOpenGL — GPU-accelerated batch renderers (glyphs, polylines, rectangles)
Plots/Common — Reusable Qt widgets (GlyphStyleControls, LineStyleControls, ColormapControls, PlotTooltipManager, axis widgets, PlotInteractionHelpers)
AutoParamWidget — Schema-driven auto-generated parameter forms
ParameterSchema — Compile-time schema extraction from reflect-cpp structs

Media_Widget duplicates significant portions of this infrastructure. Adding new features is difficult because the rendering pipeline, interaction handling, and UI controls are tightly coupled.


The motivating feature — plotting data (masks, lines, points) when no media is loaded — is blocked not by a hard technical limitation, but by entanglement. The canvas size is already independent of media resolution (driven by QGraphicsView widget size), and _clearMedia() just fills black. The real issues are:

The _plotMediaData() method has interleaved concerns: media rendering, transparency mask application, colormap processing, and multi-media compositing
The overlay rendering methods (_plotLineData, _plotMaskData, etc.) use aspect-ratio scaling factors derived from media dimensions for coordinate conversion
There’s no explicit “canvas-only mode” — the widget treats media absence as “nothing to show” rather than “show overlays on blank canvas”

title: Media_Widget Refactoring Roadmap
text:
These can be done independently, in any order, without touching the rendering pipeline.


Status: ✅ Complete
Replaced bespoke ColorPicker_Widget, point size slider/spinbox, and marker shape combo box with an embedded GlyphStyleControls + GlyphStyleState instance. PointMarkerShape enum was removed; PointDisplayOptions::marker_shape now uses CorePlotting::GlyphType directly. The color, alpha, and thickness controls are now provided by the reusable LineStyleControls widget from Plots/Common/LineStyleControls/. What exists (5 bespoke selection widgets):







Widget
Parameters




LineAddSelectionWidget
edge_snapping (bool), smoothing_mode (enum), polynomial_order (int), edge_threshold (double), edge_search_radius (double)

These have simple scalar/bool/enum parameters that map directly to ParameterSchema + AutoParamWidget. The same pattern already works for media processing options.
Not a good candidate: LineDrawAllFramesSelectionWidget has a stateful workflow (start drawing → accumulate points → complete → apply). This is genuinely interactive, not just parameter configuration.

These changes address the immediate pain point of rendering without media.


Current state:
The coordinate mapping has three interacting pieces:

Canvas pixel dimensions (_canvasWidth, _canvasHeight): fixed at 640×480 by default. This is the QGraphicsScene / QImage backing size. Media frames are scaled to this size.
Canvas coordinate system: the logical resolution that overlay data coordinates are interpreted against. Currently this is implicitly the active media’s native resolution (e.g., 640×480 for a 640×480 video). getXAspect() = _canvasWidth / media.getWidth() and getYAspect() = _canvasHeight / media.getHeight().
Per-data ImageSize: LineData, PointData, and MaskData each carry an ImageSize (from RaggedTimeSeries). If defined (not -1,‑1), the overlay rendering substitutes this for the media resolution, computing xAspect = _canvasWidth / data.getImageSize().width. If undefined (-1,‑1), the data trusts the media resolution.

Key behaviors to preserve (and formalize):

MediaData is always “correct”: its native resolution defines the authoritative canvas coordinate system when loaded. (Note: MediaData defaults to 640×480 when uninitialized — it never uses -1,‑1 — so an empty media object silently produces a coordinate system that may not match loaded overlay data.)
ImageSize -1,‑1 means “undefined”: data objects with undefined image size defer to the canvas coordinate system (currently media).
Scaling is “stretch to fill”, not “spatial subset”: when PointData has ImageSize 256×256 and media is 640×480, the points are scaled up so the 256×256 grid fills the full canvas. The implicit assumption is that the lower-resolution data represents the same spatial extent at coarser sampling, not a 256×256 crop of the 640×480 field of view. There is currently no way to express the alternative interpretation.

Problems this creates for no-media mode:

The program launches with empty MediaData whose size defaults to 640×480. If overlay data (e.g., masks at 512×512) is loaded without media, getXAspect() returns 1.0 (because no visible media → fallback), which silently misaligns data that expects coordinate mapping.
There is no explicit “canvas coordinate system” object — it is scattered across getXAspect(), getYAspect(), and per-overlay ad-hoc scaling logic, making it impossible for the user to inspect or override.
There is no mechanism for a data object to declare whether it should be stretched to fill the canvas or whether it represents a spatial subset (crop / ROI) of the canvas coordinates.

Approach:

Introduce CanvasCoordinateSystem — a small struct holding the logical { width, height } that defines the coordinate space overlays are plotted into. This replaces the implicit “ask the active media for its resolution” pattern.
Resolution priority chain — the canvas coordinate system should be determined by the first source that provides a valid (non -1,‑1) resolution, in this order:

User override (explicit manual setting via UI / state — highest priority)
Active media (MediaData::getImageSize(), if visible and not default-only)
First loaded data object with defined ImageSize (e.g., a MaskData at 512×512)
Fallback default (640×480, matching the current behavior)

When media is loaded/unloaded or data objects are added/removed, the coordinate system should be re-evaluated unless there is an active user override.
Per-data coordinate mapping mode — add a per-data-object setting (likely in the display options, e.g., PointDisplayOptions, LineDisplayOptions, MaskDisplayOptions) that controls how the data’s ImageSize relates to the canvas:








Mode
Meaning
Scaling




ScaleToCanvas (default)
Data covers the full canvas extent at its own resolution. Equivalent to current behavior.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / data.imageSize.width


SubsetOfCanvas
Data occupies a spatial sub-region. Coordinates are in canvas-coordinate-system units already.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / canvasCoordSystem.width (same as media-based scaling)



ScaleToCanvas preserves backward compatibility: data at 256×256 is stretched to fill a 640×480 canvas. SubsetOfCanvas allows, e.g., a 256×256 point cloud that lives in the top-left quadrant of a 640×480 canvas.
When ImageSize is -1,‑1, the mode is moot — the data uses the canvas coordinate system directly (equivalent to SubsetOfCanvas with matching dimensions).
Replace getXAspect() / getYAspect() — these methods currently encode the full priority chain in an ad-hoc way. Replace them with a single method (or free function) that takes CanvasCoordinateSystem, the data’s ImageSize, and the mapping mode, returning the x/y scale factors. All _plotXxxData() methods call this instead of computing their own scaling.
UI for canvas coordinate system — expose the resolved canvas coordinate system in the Media_Widget UI (read-only display showing source: “from media”, “from MaskData ‘whiskers’”, “manual override”). Provide width/height spinboxes for manual override. This can live in MediaWidgetState as a serializable field.

Status: ✅ Complete
Sub-tasks: - [x] Define CanvasCoordinateSystem struct — src/CorePlotting/Layout/CanvasCoordinateSystem.hpp - [x] Define CoordinateMappingMode enum (ScaleToCanvas, SubsetOfCanvas) — same file - [x] Add CoordinateMappingMode field to LineDisplayOptions, PointDisplayOptions, MaskDisplayOptions (default: ScaleToCanvas) — DisplayOptions.hpp - [x] Add CanvasCoordinateSystem to MediaWidgetState (with optional user override) — MediaWidgetStateData.hpp, MediaWidgetState.hpp/.cpp - [x] Implement resolution priority chain in Media_Window::resolveCanvasCoordinateSystem() — called at the top of each UpdateCanvas(); priority: user override → active media → first data object with defined ImageSize → 640×480 fallback - [x] Replace getXAspect() / getYAspect() with unified scaling function — computeScalingFactors() / computeInverseScalingFactors() free functions in CanvasCoordinateSystem.hpp; getXAspect()/getYAspect() kept as backward-compatible wrappers (used by MediaLine_Widget.cpp) - [x] Update all _plotXxxData() and hit-testing methods to use new scaling function — _plotLineData, _plotPointData, _plotMaskData (bounding box), _findLineAtPosition, _findPointAtPosition (bug fix: was ignoring ImageSize entirely), _findMaskAtPosition, updateTemporaryLine (bug fix: fetched ImageSize but never used it) - [x] Add UI controls in Media_Widget for viewing/overriding canvas coordinate system — CanvasCoord_Widget in Media_Widget/UI/, integrated into MediaPropertiesWidget as a collapsible section; shows resolved width×height and source, with manual override via QCheckBox + QSpinBox pair - [x] Unit tests for coordinate mapping (pure math, no Qt dependency) — tests/CorePlotting/CanvasCoordinateSystem.test.cpp, 19 test cases / 44 assertions
This is the key unlock — once the canvas coordinate system is an explicit, inspectable, overridable entity, overlay rendering becomes independent of media presence, and plotting without media becomes trivial.



Completed prerequisite: Media_Widget::setDataManager() now calls updateMedia() at the end of setup, wiring the QGraphicsScene to the QGraphicsView immediately on widget creation. Previously this was only called from MainWindow::loadData(), which meant overlays were invisible until the user loaded a media file. The legacy loop in MainWindow::loadData() has been removed.
Remaining approach: 1. Add a bool _has_media flag or derive from whether any media data key is registered 2. In UpdateCanvas(): if no media, skip _plotMediaData() but still render all overlays 3. Allow background color configuration (currently hardcoded black) 4. Support user-specified canvas dimensions via state when no media is loaded
Estimated scope: ~50 lines — mostly guard changes in UpdateCanvas() and _plotMediaData(), plus a state field for “background_color”



Current state: - getXAspect(), getYAspect(), _getMediaScaledPosition() are methods on Media_Window - Each overlay type has its own scaling logic scattered through 1800+ lines of Media_Window.cpp
Approach: 1. Create a free-function utility: CanvasPoint mapToCanvas(DataPoint, CanvasCoordinateSystem, DataBounds) 2. Use it in all _plotXxxData() methods 3. This also makes it testable without Qt (unit tests for coordinate math)





These integrate Media_Widget’s rendering with the modern stack.


Current state: - _plotLineData() manually iterates LineData, creates QPainterPath, scales coordinates - _plotPointData() manually creates QGraphicsItems per marker shape - _plotMaskData() manually iterates Mask2D pixels, creates QImages

Approach: 1. After mapping data with CorePlotting mappers (3.1), build a RenderableScene with spatial index 2. Replace _findXxxAtPosition() methods with SceneHitTester::hitTest() 3. Unifies all selection to one code path

title: MediaProcessingPipeline
text: MediaProcessingPipeline is a lightweight, Qt-free static library that provides a registry of image processing steps. It bridges the ImageProcessing library’s option structs with the ParameterSchema/AutoParamWidget system, enabling auto-generated UIs for processing parameters.

title: MediaProcessingPipeline
text: MediaProcessingPipeline is a lightweight, Qt-free static library that provides a registry of image processing steps. It bridges the ImageProcessing library’s option structs with the ParameterSchema/AutoParamWidget system, enabling auto-generated UIs for processing parameters.

title: MediaProcessingPipeline
text:
Location
src/MediaProcessingPipeline/

title: MediaProcessingPipeline
text:
Dependencies

ImageProcessing — option structs and processing functions
ParameterSchema — extractParameterSchema<T>() and ParameterUIHints<T>
reflectcpp — struct reflection for schema extraction

title: MediaProcessingPipeline
text:
Key Components

ProcessingOptionsSchema.hpp
Companion header providing ParameterUIHints<T> specializations for each processing option struct defined in ImageProcessing/ProcessingOptions.hpp. This keeps the rfl dependency out of ImageProcessing while adding UI annotations (tooltips, value ranges) for AutoParamWidget.
Annotated structs:

ContrastOptions — alpha/beta/display range
GammaOptions — gamma value
SharpenOptions — sigma
ClaheOptions — grid size, clip limit
BilateralOptions — diameter, color/spatial sigma
MedianOptions — kernel size
MagicEraserParams — brush size, median filter size
ColormapOptions — colormap type, alpha, normalize



ProcessingStep.hpp
Descriptor struct for a named processing step:

display_name — human-readable name for UI sections
chain_key — key used with MediaData::addProcessingStep() (e.g., "1__lineartransform")
schema — ParameterSchema for auto-generating the parameter UI
apply — type-erased function void(cv::Mat&, nlohmann::json const&) that applies the step



ProcessingStepRegistry
Singleton registry mapping step names to ProcessingStep descriptors. Steps register at static-initialization time via the RegisterStep<Params> RAII helper (same pattern as DataSynthesizer’s RegisterGenerator and TransformsV2’s static registration).
// Example registration
static RegisterStep<ContrastOptions> const reg_contrast{
    "Linear Transform",
    "1__lineartransform",
    [](cv::Mat& m, ContrastOptions const& o) { ImageProcessing::linear_transform(m, o); }
};
Currently registered steps: Linear Transform, Gamma Correction, Image Sharpening, CLAHE, Bilateral Filter, Median Filter. Magic Eraser and Colormap are handled specially due to their state/rendering requirements.

title: MediaProcessingPipeline
text:
Design Rationale
This library exists to support the phased refactoring of MediaProcessing_Widget from hand-written per-filter widgets to AutoParamWidget-driven generic UI. See the refactoring roadmap for the full plan.

title: KeymapSystem Library Reference
text: The KeymapSystem static library (src/WhiskerToolbox/KeymapSystem/) provides the core infrastructure for configurable, context-aware keyboard shortcuts. It implements action registration, scope-based resolution, user override management, and conflict detection.

title: KeymapSystem Library Reference
text: The KeymapSystem static library (src/WhiskerToolbox/KeymapSystem/) provides the core infrastructure for configurable, context-aware keyboard shortcuts. It implements action registration, scope-based resolution, user override management, and conflict detection.

title: KeymapSystem Library Reference
text:
Files

KeyAction.hpp
Defines the core action types:

KeyActionScopeKind — Enum: Global, EditorFocused, AlwaysRouted
KeyActionScope — Pairs a scope kind with an optional EditorTypeId. Factory methods: global(), editorFocused(type_id), alwaysRouted(type_id)
KeyActionDescriptor — Pure metadata for a bindable action: action_id, display_name, category, scope, and default_binding



Keymap.hpp
Defines binding types:

KeymapEntry — Runtime resolved binding (action → key sequence, enabled flag, override flag)
KeymapOverrideEntry — Serializable user override using std::string for reflect-cpp compatibility. Stored in AppPreferencesData for persistence.



KeyActionAdapter.hpp / KeyActionAdapter.cpp
Composition-based component for receiving keymap dispatches. Widgets create a KeyActionAdapter as a child QObject and install a handler lambda. No inheritance required.
Key API:

setHandler(Handler) — Install callback std::function<bool(QString const &)>
handleKeyAction(action_id) — Called by KeymapManager to dispatch
setInstanceId() / setTypeId() — Associate with an editor instance/type



KeymapManager.hpp / KeymapManager.cpp
Central manager class (owned by MainWindow). Inherits QObject.
Registration API:

registerAction(descriptor) — Register action metadata (returns false on duplicate)
unregisterAction(action_id) — Remove action and its override

Query API:

allActions() — All registered descriptors
action(action_id) — Lookup by ID
bindingFor(action_id) — Effective key (override > default)
isActionEnabled(action_id) — Check enabled state

Override API:

setUserOverride(action_id, key) — Override key binding
clearUserOverride(action_id) — Revert to default
clearAllOverrides() — Reset all customizations
setActionEnabled(action_id, enabled) — Enable/disable

Resolution API:

resolveKeyPress(key, focused_type_id) — Scope-priority resolution: EditorFocused > AlwaysRouted > Global
detectConflicts() — Find same-key/same-scope collisions

Adapter routing:

registerAdapter(adapter) — Register for dispatch (auto-deregisters on destruction)
dispatchAction(action_id, target_type, target_instance) — Route to matching adapter

Serialization:

exportOverrides() / importOverrides(overrides) — Round-trip persistence

Signal: bindingsChanged() — emitted on any binding modification.
Event filter (installed on QApplication by MainWindow):

title: Keybinding Editor
text: The KeybindingEditor is a dock widget that allows users to view and customize all registered keyboard shortcuts. It reads from and writes to KeymapManager, providing a full GUI for the Keymap System’s override management.

title: Keybinding Editor
text: The KeybindingEditor is a dock widget that allows users to view and customize all registered keyboard shortcuts. It reads from and writes to KeymapManager, providing a full GUI for the Keymap System’s override management.

title: Keybinding Editor
text:
Architecture
The editor is composed of three internal components:

KeymapModel
QAbstractItemModel subclass that provides a two-level tree structure:

Level 0 (Category): Groups actions by their KeyActionDescriptor::category field (e.g., “Timeline”, “Media Viewer”, “Application”)
Level 1 (Action): Individual actions within each category

Columns:







Column
Contents




Action
Display name (bold for categories)


Binding
Current effective binding (blue italic if overridden, red if conflicting)


Scope
Global, Focused (TypeId), or Always (TypeId)


Default
The shipped default binding



Custom roles:








Role
Type
Description




ActionIdRole
QString
The action_id for action rows; empty for categories


IsCategoryRole
bool
true for category rows


HasConflictRole
bool
true if this action participates in a binding conflict


IsOverrideRole
bool
true if user override differs from default



The model calls KeymapManager::allActions() and KeymapManager::detectConflicts() on each refresh(). Refresh is triggered automatically by KeymapManager::bindingsChanged().


KeySequenceRecorder
A QPushButton subclass that captures keyboard input:

User clicks “Record” → button enters recording mode (yellow highlight, “Press a key…” text)
Button grabs keyboard focus
Next key press (with modifiers) is captured as a QKeySequence
keySequenceRecorded(QKeySequence) signal is emitted
Button returns to normal state

Special behaviors:

Escape cancels recording without emitting a result
Bare modifier keys (Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Meta alone) are ignored — recording waits for a real key
Focus loss auto-cancels recording



KeybindingEditor
The main widget composed of:

Search bar (QLineEdit) — filters the tree by action name using QSortFilterProxyModel with recursive filtering
Tree view (QTreeView) — displays the KeymapModel through the proxy
Record button (KeySequenceRecorder) — captures a new key for the selected action
Clear button — unbinds the selected action (sets empty QKeySequence as override)
Reset button — reverts the selected action to its default binding
Reset All button — clears all overrides (with confirmation dialog)

title: Keybinding Editor
text:
Data Flow
KeymapManager ──allActions()──→ KeymapModel ──→ QSortFilterProxyModel ──→ QTreeView
    ↑                                                                        │
    │                                                                        │
    └────setUserOverride()────── KeybindingEditor ←──── user interaction ─────┘
    └────clearUserOverride()──── KeybindingEditor
    └────clearAllOverrides()──── KeybindingEditor
Changes flow back through KeymapManager::bindingsChanged() signal, which triggers KeymapModel::refresh() and persistence to AppPreferencesData.

title: Developer Documentation
text:
Welcome to the developer documentation for Neuralyzer. This is a C++ project for data analysis and visualization focused on the multi-modal data found in Systems Neuroscience. While higher level languages like MATLAB or Python are more common in our field, C++ was selected for this package to hide the programming aspects from the average user so that it “just works”. However, if you are here, you most likely want to try to modify Neuralyzer in some way. If you are new to C++, I have collected resouces that helped me to learn in the Intro to C++ section.
The Build Instructions section has a guide with getting an operational, developmental version of Neuralyzer on your own machine.
Once you have a working version of Neuralyzer, I recommend checking out the design guidelines and code quality section. It contains the design specifications and rules for writing C++ code for this project. It also contains descriptions of some of the tooling that can do most of this for you.
For starting projects, I recommend looking into four separate initiatives to ensure Neuralyzer remains performant and robust. These are good starting points to learn more about how Neuralyzer works under the hood:

Testing: Unit tests are critical for ensuring that code changes do not break existing functionality. This section describes the testing framework and guidelines for writing tests.
Profiling and Performance: Profiling tools can help identify performance bottlenecks in the code. This section describes how to use profiling tools to optimize code performance.
Static Analysis: Static analysis tools can help identify potential issues in the code before they become problems. This section describes how to use static analysis tools to improve code quality.
Fuzzing: Fuzzing is a technique for testing software by providing random inputs to the program. This section describes how to use fuzzing to identify bugs in the code or unexpected edge cases in complex algorithms.

Neuralyzer has many moving parts. There are multiple libraries that encapsulate different features that are maintained as part of this project. It is worth being familiar with some of these:

CoreGeometry:
CorePlotting: This is the backend agnostic plotting interface for
Entity:
TimeFrame:
