Despite the different data sources, significant infrastructure is shared:

Colormap system (Phase 2)
Colorbar widget (Phase 4)
Sorting modes (Phase 6) — time-to-peak, peak value, etc.
Cross-widget linking (Phase 7) — click row → update linked widgets
PNG/SVG export (Phase 10)
Scaling/normalization (Phase 3) — z-score, 0-1 normalization




Key differences that may warrant a separate widget rather than a mode switch:

Data gathering: GatherResult<AnalogTimeSeries> instead of GatherResult<DigitalEventSeries>
Value computation: Direct sampling/interpolation instead of binning + rate estimation
Alignment: May align to DigitalIntervalSeries only (baseline period for ΔF/F₀ normalization)
Time resolution: Native sampling rate rather than binned; may need downsampling for display
Tooltip: Would show a line trace rather than a PSTH histogram




Implement as a separate widget (AnalogHeatmapWidget) that reuses the colormap, colorbar, sorting, linking, and export infrastructure. The rendering and data gathering paths are sufficiently different that forcing them into a single widget would add unwanted complexity. The two widgets can coexist in the Plot menu, clearly labeled:

Plot → Heatmap Plot (Events) — current widget
Plot → Heatmap Plot (Analog) — future widget






Row label rendering: Should unit labels be rendered as axis tick labels via VerticalAxisWidget, or as a separate label column? The axis approach reuses existing infrastructure but may not handle long labels well.
Performance at scale: What is the target unit count? 100 units × 200 bins = 20K rectangles is trivial for OpenGL. 1000 units × 1000 bins = 1M rectangles may need texture-based rendering instead of rectangle batches.
AnalogTimeSeries variant timing: Should the analog heatmap be a mode of this widget or a completely separate widget? The shared infrastructure is substantial, but the data pipelines are fundamentally different.

title: Heatmap Widget Roadmap
text:
The following features are complete and documented in index.qmd:

State management: HeatmapState with PlotAlignmentState, RelativeTimeAxisState, VerticalAxisState composition

Y-axis auto-fit: HeatmapWidget auto-fits the vertical axis when the unit count changes. Y bounds are set to [0, num_units], Y zoom is reset to 1.0, and Y pan is reset to 0.0 so all units are visible. The VerticalAxisWidget uses identityAxis("Unit", 0) for integer unit-index labels. Signal renamed from trialCountChanged to unitCountChanged for semantic clarity.

Sorting logic in HeatmapDataPipeline.hpp/cpp via computeSortOrder() (returns index permutation) and applySortOrder() (reorders rows, rate estimates, and unit keys in-place). Applied after runHeatmapPipeline() in renderer before colormap mapping. Properties panel has “Sorting” collapsible section with sort mode combo and ascending checkbox. Full serialization round-trip.

Goal: Allow the user to export the current onion skin view as an SVG file, preserving vector quality for publication.


SVG export requires converting the OpenGL scene to vector graphics. Two approaches:
Option A — Scene-to-SVG serialization (recommended): Walk the RenderableScene primitives (glyphs, polylines) and emit SVG <circle>, <polygon>, and <polyline> elements with the same colors and alpha values computed during rebuildScene(). This avoids OpenGL framebuffer capture and produces clean, resolution-independent output.
Option B — QPainter-based rendering: Use QSvgGenerator + QPainter to re-render the scene data using Qt’s 2D drawing API. This provides more mature vector rendering but requires duplicating the rendering logic outside OpenGL.

title: PSTH Widget
text: The PSTH Widget renders Peri-Stimulus Time Histogram plots showing the rate or count of discrete events (spikes, behavioral markers) aggregated across multiple trials, aligned to a user-selected reference event or interval. Users can overlay multiple DigitalEventSeries, configure bin size and plot style (bar chart or line), and interact with the plot via zoom and pan. The histogram aggregates event counts across all trials into uniformly spaced time bins relative to the alignment point (t = 0).

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Component Overview







Component
Responsibility




PSTHWidget (UI)
Top-level Qt widget — composes OpenGL canvas, relative time axis, vertical axis


PSTHPropertiesWidget (UI)
Properties panel — alignment settings, event series management, style/bin size, color picker


PSTHPlotOpenGLWidget (Rendering)
OpenGL canvas — histogram binning, scene building, rendering, mouse interaction


PSTHState (Core)
Serializable state — alignment, view state, per-event options, bin size, plot style


PSTHWidgetRegistration
Registers type with EditorRegistry (state, view, properties factories)

title: PSTH Widget
text:
EditorState Pattern
The PSTH Widget follows the project’s EditorState architecture:

PSTHState inherits from EditorState
Registered with EditorRegistry via PSTHWidgetModule::registerTypes()
PSTHWidget is the view factory, PSTHPropertiesWidget is the properties factory
Both share the same PSTHState instance
Properties placed in Right zone, view placed in Center zone (default)
The create_editor_custom factory in PSTHWidgetRegistration handles coupling the view and properties widgets (e.g., connecting range controls)

title: PSTH Widget
PSTH Widget
PSTH Widget
text:
Plot Style
The widget supports two rendering styles via the PSTHStyle enum:







Style
Description




Bar
Classic bar chart (default). Each bin rendered as a filled rectangle via HistogramMapper::toBars().


Line
Step-function line connecting bin tops via HistogramMapper::toLine(). Produces a classic histogram outline.



Both styles use the shared CorePlotting::HistogramMapper infrastructure that is also used by ACFWidget.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Signal Architecture
PSTHState emits category-level signals to minimize coupling complexity:







Signal
Trigger




alignmentEventKeyChanged
Alignment event/interval key changed


intervalAlignmentTypeChanged
Interval alignment type changed


offsetChanged
Alignment offset changed


windowSizeChanged
Window size changed (also resets zoom/pan)


plotEventAdded / plotEventRemoved / plotEventOptionsChanged
Per-event series changes


styleChanged
Bar ↔︎ Line style switch


estimationParamsChanged
Estimation method or parameters changed


scalingChanged
Normalization/scaling mode changed


viewStateChanged
Zoom, pan, or bounds changed (view transform only — no scene rebuild)


stateChanged (inherited)
Any change requiring scene rebuild



Performance-critical separation: Zoom and pan operations emit only viewStateChanged(), which updates the projection matrix without triggering an expensive scene rebuild via stateChanged().

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Composition with PlotAlignmentState
PSTHState owns a PlotAlignmentState instance that manages alignment settings (event key, interval alignment type, offset, window size). This is the same shared component used by EventPlotWidget and HeatmapWidget, ensuring consistent alignment behavior across all trial-aligned plot types.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Composition with Axis States
PSTHState owns both:

RelativeTimeAxisState — for the X-axis (relative time centered at t = 0). Synchronized bidirectionally with the view state, using the “silent update” pattern described in the Plot Widget Guide.
VerticalAxisState — for the Y-axis (event count). The Y bounds are auto-adjusted when the scene rebuilds to accommodate the maximum bin count (with 10% padding). Uses identityAxis("Count", 0) mapping for integer labels.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Data Flow
PSTHState (alignment settings + bin size + per-event options)
        ↓
GatherResult<DigitalEventSeries> (trial-aligned views)
        ↓
Event binning: events → histogram counts per bin
        ↓
CorePlotting::HistogramData (bin_start, bin_width, counts[])
        ↓
CorePlotting::HistogramMapper::buildScene() → RenderableScene
        ↓
PlottingOpenGL::SceneRenderer::render()

title: PSTH Widget
text:
GatherResult Integration
Trial alignment uses the shared GatherResult infrastructure from DataManager. The PSTHPlotOpenGLWidget::rebuildScene() method:

Reads alignment settings from PSTHState::alignmentState()
For each configured event series, calls WhiskerToolbox::Plots::createAlignedGatherResult<DigitalEventSeries>() using the shared PlotAlignmentGather utility
Iterates over all trials in the GatherResult, converting each event’s TimeFrameIndex to absolute time via the source series’ TimeFrame
Computes relative time (event time − alignment time) for each event
Assigns events to histogram bins based on relative time

This is the same GatherResult pattern used by EventPlotWidget (for per-trial views) and HeatmapWidget (for aggregated heat values). The pattern of going from aligned spike times to aggregated rate/count via GatherResult is directly reusable for the HeatmapWidget’s firing rate computation.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Histogram Binning
Bins are computed in rebuildScene():

Bin range: [-window_size/2, +window_size/2]
Number of bins: ceil(window_size / bin_size)
Bin assignment: floor((relative_time + half_window) / bin_size), clamped to [0, num_bins - 1]
Y-axis auto-fit: After computing histogram counts, the vertical axis y_max is set to max_count * 1.1 to provide padding above the tallest bar

The binning currently produces raw event counts (sum across all trials). See the PSTH Roadmap for planned normalization modes (firing rate, spike probability) and smoothing algorithms.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Scene Building
The PSTHPlotOpenGLWidget manages the full rendering lifecycle:

Scene rebuild (on stateChanged): Gathers trial data, bins events into HistogramData, maps to geometry via HistogramMapper, and uploads to SceneRenderer
View update (on viewStateChanged): Updates only the projection matrix — no data re-gathering
Paint (on paintGL): Renders the cached scene through PlottingOpenGL::SceneRenderer

A _updating_y_max_from_rebuild flag prevents feedback loops when the scene rebuild updates the vertical axis bounds.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Shared Histogram Infrastructure
The histogram rendering pipeline is decoupled from the PSTH-specific logic:



Component
Location
Shared With




HistogramData
CorePlotting/DataTypes/
ACFWidget


HistogramMapper
CorePlotting/Mappers/
ACFWidget


HistogramStyle
CorePlotting/Mappers/
ACFWidget


RenderableRectangleBatch
CorePlotting/SceneGraph/
All OpenGL widgets


RenderablePolyLineBatch
CorePlotting/SceneGraph/
All OpenGL widgets



HistogramMapper converts HistogramData into either a RenderableRectangleBatch (bar mode) or a RenderablePolyLineBatch (line mode), which is then uploaded to the SceneRenderer. This same infrastructure is reused by ACFWidget for autocorrelation and ISI histogram rendering.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Zoom and Pan
The widget supports separated X/Y zoom for independent exploration of time and count dimensions, using the shared PlotInteractionHelpers:



Input
Action




Mouse wheel
X-zoom only (time axis)


Shift + wheel
Y-zoom only (count axis)


Ctrl + wheel
Uniform zoom (both axes)


Click + drag
Pan in both axes



The interaction delegates to WhiskerToolbox::Plots::handlePanning() and WhiskerToolbox::Plots::handleZoom() from PlotInteractionHelpers.hpp, which are shared across all OpenGL plot widgets. A DRAG_THRESHOLD of 4 pixels prevents accidental pans during clicks.
Zoom and pan update only the view projection (no scene rebuild), providing smooth interactive performance.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Double Click
Double-clicking emits plotDoubleClicked(time_frame_index), which the parent PSTHWidget converts to a TimePosition and forwards to EditorRegistry::setCurrentTime(). This navigates other time-synced widgets to the clicked time position. The world-to-time conversion is currently a stub (emits index 0).

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Time Axis (X)
Uses the shared RelativeTimeAxisWidget with RelativeTimeAxisState. The axis is synchronized bidirectionally with the view state:

User changes axis range → view state updates → scene rebuilds (via rangeChanged)
User zooms/pans → axis range updates silently via setRangeSilent() (no feedback loop)

The axis uses CorePlotting::relativeTimeAxis() mapping for “+N” / “−N” / “0” label formatting.
See Plot Widget Guide for full axis integration details including the “Silent Update” pattern.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Count Axis (Y)
Uses VerticalAxisWidget with VerticalAxisState. The Y bounds are auto-adjusted when the histogram is rebuilt:

After computing bin counts, y_max is set to max_count * 1.1
This triggers a vertical axis range update via VerticalAxisState::setYMax()
The axis uses CorePlotting::identityAxis("Count", 0) mapping for integer labels

Both axis widgets provide collapsible range control sections (RelativeTimeAxisRangeControls and VerticalAxisRangeControls) that are inserted into the properties panel when setPlotWidget() is called.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Alignment Section
Uses the shared PlotAlignmentWidget component (same as EventPlot and Heatmap). Provides:

Alignment event combo box (populated with DigitalEventSeries and DigitalIntervalSeries keys)
Interval alignment type (Beginning/End)
Offset control
Window size control

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Global Options

Style combo box: Bar or Line rendering mode
Estimation method controls: Uses shared EstimationMethodControls widget from RateEstimationControls library. Supports binning (default), Gaussian kernel, and causal exponential estimation methods. Each method has its own parameter page in a stacked widget.
Scaling mode controls: Uses shared ScalingModeControls widget from RateEstimationControls library. Supports Raw Count (default), Firing Rate (Hz), Z-Score, Normalized [0,1], and Count/Trial normalization modes.

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Event Series Management

Add event combo box: Lists available DigitalEventSeries keys from DataManager
Add/Remove buttons: Manage the set of overlaid event series
Plot events table: Two-column table (Event Name, Data Key) showing current series
Per-event color picker: Color button + display swatch for the selected event

title: PSTH Widget
text:
Axis Range Controls
Collapsible sections for both time axis and vertical axis range controls, created when setPlotWidget() connects the properties widget to the view widget.

title: PSTH Widget
PSTH Widget
text:
Data Retrieval
The OpenGL widget retrieves event data via DataManager::getData<DigitalEventSeries>(key) and accesses the source series’ TimeFrame for absolute time conversion during binning. Null checks are performed at each stage to handle deleted or missing keys gracefully.

title: Neuralyzer
section: Known Bug Patterns (check all plot widgets)
text:
Known Bug Patterns (check all plot widgets)

1. markDirty() in view-only setters causes scene rebuilds on zoom/pan
EditorState::markDirty() always emits stateChanged(). If view-only setters (setXZoom, setYZoom, setPan) call markDirty(), the connected onStateChanged() slot sets _scene_dirty = true, causing a full scene rebuild on every zoom/pan frame. The comments in these setters often say “No stateChanged() here” but markDirty() emits it anyway.
Fix: Remove markDirty() from view-only setters. The view state is still written to _data.view_state for serialization; it will be saved when the next real state change calls markDirty().
Fixed in: EventPlotState (setXZoom, setYZoom, setPan)
Check: LinePlotState and any other plot state classes with the same pattern.


2. rangeUpdated handler emits stateChanged() causing rebuild on resize/pan
RelativeTimeAxisState::setRangeSilent() emits rangeUpdated. If the state class’s rangeUpdated handler calls markDirty() → stateChanged(), this creates a cascade: resize → paintGL → viewBoundsChanged → syncTimeAxisRange() → setRangeSilent() → rangeUpdated → markDirty() → stateChanged() → _scene_dirty = true → full scene rebuild.
Fix: The rangeUpdated handler should only sync serialization data (_data.time_axis = ...) without calling markDirty() or emitting stateChanged().
Fixed in: EventPlotState
Check: LinePlotState and any other state class connecting to rangeUpdated.

title: Scatter Plot Widget Roadmap
text:
This document tracks remaining development tasks for the Scatter Plot Widget. For documentation of completed features and current architecture, see the main developer documentation.
Not yet implemented: Stale key handling (Phase 6.3).



Status: Complete. All widget integration steps finished.
Goal: Color scatter points by an external data source (e.g., velocity colored by acceleration, points colored by whether they fall inside a DigitalIntervalSeries interval).


The shared CorePlotting/FeatureColor/ library is fully implemented and tested (24 test cases, 74 assertions). See the FeatureColor module docs for the full API reference. Key components:

FeatureColorSourceDescriptor — serializable pointer to a DataManager key + optional column
resolveFeatureColors() — per-point float lookup via ATS, TensorData (TFI hash join / ordinal positional), or DIS containment
checkFeatureColorCompatibility() — validates key existence, column existence, row-type compatibility
applyFeatureColorsToScene() — mutates RenderableGlyphBatch::colors[] via ContinuousMapping (colormap) or ThresholdMapping (binary)
computeEffectiveColorRange() — Auto/Manual/Symmetric vmin/vmax from resolved values
PlotSourceRowType — shared enum (replaces the earlier ScatterSourceRowType)




Feature coloring is a post-buildScatterPoints() color override inserted before group colors:
buildScatterPoints()          → ScatterPointData with time_indices
    → addGlyphs()             → uniform color from GlyphStyleData
    → applyFeatureColorsToScene()  → per-point color override (NEW)
    → applyGroupColorsToScene()    → group colors override feature colors
    → uploadScene()
No changes needed to SceneBuilder, GlyphRenderer, or shaders. Color priority (highest wins): navigate highlight > selected > group > feature > default glyph style.

title: Spectrogram Widget Roadmap
Spectrogram Widget Roadmap
text:
Status: Not started. The widget shell exists but has no rendering layer.
Goal: Add a SpectrogramOpenGLWidget that renders a time × frequency matrix as a colored image.


Create the rendering layer:
Plots/SpectrogramWidget/Rendering/
├── SpectrogramOpenGLWidget.hpp
└── SpectrogramOpenGLWidget.cpp
Following the same QOpenGLWidget lifecycle pattern as HeatmapOpenGLWidget from HeatmapWidget:

initializeGL() — initialize SceneRenderer, set background color
resizeGL() — update viewport and projection
paintGL() — render the scene via SceneRenderer
rebuildScene() — convert the spectral matrix to renderable geometry




Two options for rendering the spectrogram matrix:
Option A: Rectangle Batch Same pattern as HeatmapWidget — one RenderableRectangleBatch with one colored rectangle per cell. Simple, works well for moderate matrices (e.g., 200 time bins × 128 frequency bins = 25K rectangles).
Option B: Texture-Based Rendering Upload the color-mapped matrix as a 2D OpenGL texture and render a single textured quad. This is dramatically more efficient for large spectrograms (e.g., 1000+ time bins × 512 frequency bins). Requires a texture upload path in SceneRenderer.
Recommendation: Start with Option A (rectangle batch) for consistency with HeatmapWidget and simplicity. If performance is insufficient for large spectrograms, add texture-based rendering as an optimization in a later phase.



The rebuildScene() method:

Retrieve the TensorData spectrogram from DataManager using the configured key
Determine the visible time window from the state’s X bounds
Slice the matrix to the visible time range and frequency range
Apply the colormap to map scalar power values → RGBA colors
Build a RenderableRectangleBatch: each cell is a rectangle from (time_bin_start, freq_bin_start) to (time_bin_start + bin_width, freq_bin_start + bin_height)
Upload to SceneRenderer




Mouse interaction should use the shared PlotInteractionHelpers from Plot Widget Guide:







Input
Action




Mouse wheel
Y-zoom (frequency axis)


Shift + wheel
(reserved — X zoom triggers data reload, see Phase 3)


Click + drag
Y-pan (scroll through frequency range)


Double-click
Emit timePositionSelected for cross-widget navigation



Note: X panning is disabled because the spectrogram is centered on the global time position (see X-Axis: Centered Time). X zoom is a data operation, not a view transform, and is handled in Phase 3.

title: Spectrogram Widget Roadmap
text:
FFT library: KissFFT vs. PocketFFT vs. custom implementation? PocketFFT (header-only, BSD, derived from NumPy) is the recommended choice, but the project may prefer minimizing new dependencies.
Texture vs. rectangle rendering: For large spectrograms (1000+ time bins × 512+ frequency bins), texture-based rendering would be dramatically more efficient. Should this be implemented from the start, or should we begin with rectangle batches for consistency with HeatmapWidget and optimize later?
X zoom behavior: When the user zooms X (changing the time window), should the widget:

re-run the spectrogram transform with new bounds, or (b) pre-compute a wider spectrogram and slice it? Option (b) is faster for interactive use but requires more memory.

Shared colormap extraction timing: Should the colormap infrastructure be extracted to CorePlotting/Colormaps/ before or during SpectrogramWidget development? If HeatmapWidget Phase 2 happens first, the infrastructure will already exist. If SpectrogramWidget is developed first, it should create the shared infrastructure.
CenteredTimeAxis dependency: The SpectrogramWidget and DataViewerWidget both need the CenteredTimeAxis. Should this be extracted as a prerequisite shared component, or should each widget implement a local version and consolidate later?
AnalogTimeSeries workflow: When the user selects an AnalogTimeSeries key, should the widget automatically trigger the spectrogram transform, or should the user be expected to run the transform manually first via DataTransform_Widget and then select the resulting TensorData key?

title: Temporal Projection View Widget Roadmap
text:
This document tracks remaining development tasks for the Temporal Projection View Widget. For documentation of completed features and current architecture, see the main developer documentation.


The following features are complete and documented in index.qmd:

Widget skeleton: EditorState pattern, registration, state/view/properties factories
State management: TemporalProjectionViewState with HorizontalAxisState, VerticalAxisState composition; TemporalProjectionViewStateData serializable struct with rfl::json
Dual rendering pipeline: SceneRenderer for point glyphs, BatchLineRenderer for selectable lines
Data key management: Add/remove multiple PointData and LineData keys via properties panel
Spatial mapping: SpatialMapper::mapAllPoints() for flattening all time frames; buildLineBatchFromLineData() for line segments
Auto-fit bounds: Bounding box computation from actual data with 2% margin, zoom/pan reset on bounds change
Axis system: HorizontalAxisWidget (X) and VerticalAxisWidget (Y) with bidirectional sync, including the “silent update” pattern
Interaction: Separated X/Y zoom, pan via shared PlotInteractionHelpers
Point selection: Ctrl+Click toggle via SceneHitTester::queryQuadTree() with 10px tolerance
Line selection: Ctrl+Click drag intersection stroke via shared LineSelectionHelpers, GPU compute shader and CPU intersector backends
Selection state: std::unordered_set<EntityId> with preservation across scene rebuilds
Rendering controls: Point size and line width spinboxes in properties panel
Selection mode toggle: None / Point / Line combo box in properties panel
DataManager observer: Combo box population and cleanup in destructor
State serialization: Full round-trip JSON via rfl::json
Registration wiring: timePositionSelected → EditorRegistry::setCurrentTime() connection
Line style customization: LineStyleData (color, thickness, alpha) via LineStyleState/LineStyleControls — global single style, replaces hardcoded red
Polygon selection: Dual-mode selection (Point/Line/Polygon) via combo box; Enter to close polygon, Backspace to undo vertex, Escape to cancel; uses shared PolygonInteractionController and selectPointsInPolygon() from CorePlotting/Selection/; polygon preview via PreviewRenderer; additive selection (adds to existing)
Group integration: Right-click context menu via GroupContextMenuHandler for “Add to Group”, “Create New Group”, “Remove from Group”; integrated with EntityRegistry; selection instructions via shared SelectionInstructions helpers
Group-based coloring: color_by_group toggle in properties panel; applyGroupColorsToScene() applies group colors to point glyphs with priority (selected → group → default); GroupManager signal connections trigger scene rebuild on group changes

Not yet implemented: double-click time navigation, subgroup visibility filtering, per-key rendering options described below.




Status: Not started. The mouseDoubleClickEvent handler exists but delegates to the base class. The timePositionSelected signal is already wired to EditorRegistry::setCurrentTime() via the registration.
Goal: Double-clicking on a point or line should navigate other time-synced widgets to the associated time position.


When in point selection mode and the user double-clicks on a point glyph:

Perform hit testing via SceneHitTester::queryQuadTree() (same as single-click)
Look up the EntityId for the hit point
Resolve the EntityId → TimeFrameIndex mapping from the PointData source
Convert TimeFrameIndex → TimePosition via the TimeFrame
Emit timePositionSelected(position) → EditorRegistry::setCurrentTime()

This is the same navigation pattern used by EventPlotWidget (eventDoubleClicked → setCurrentTime()).



When in line selection mode and the user double-clicks near a line:

Find the nearest line segment to the click position
Look up the EntityId for that line
Resolve the EntityId → TimeFrameIndex mapping from the LineData source
Convert to TimePosition and emit timePositionSelected




During scene building, construct a lookup from EntityId to its source time frame index. Both PointData and LineData store per-entry time indices, so the mapping can be built during the rebuildScene() pass and cached as std::unordered_map<EntityId, TimeFrameIndex>.





Status: Not started. Depends on Phase 5 (group integration) and Phase 6 (group coloring).
Goal: Allow the user to selectively show/hide points and lines by their group membership, enabling focused analysis of specific subgroups.


Extend state with a visibility filter:
struct TemporalProjectionViewStateData {
    // ... existing fields ...

    // Groups to show. Empty means "show all".
    std::vector<std::string> visible_groups;
    bool show_ungrouped = true;  ///< Show entities not in any group
};



In rebuildScene(), before building the scene, filter entities:
For points:

After SpatialMapper::mapAllPoints(), iterate MappedElement objects
For each element, check if its EntityId belongs to a visible group
Only include matching elements in the SceneBuilder::addGlyphs() call

For lines:

After building LineBatchData, set visibility_mask[i] = 0 for lines whose EntityId does not belong to a visible group
Upload the filtered visibility mask to BatchLineStore

The BatchLineRenderer already respects the visibility mask, so no rendering changes are needed for lines.



Add a “Visibility” collapsible section:

Group checklist — checkbox per group (checked = visible)
“Show ungrouped” checkbox — toggle visibility of entities not in any group
“Show All” / “Hide All” buttons — convenience toggles




User toggles group visibility checkbox
        ↓
State updates visible_groups
        ↓
stateChanged() emitted
        ↓
rebuildScene() filters by visibility
        ↓
Filtered scene rendered





Status: Not started. Currently rendering options (point size, line width, color) are global.
Goal: Allow per-data-key rendering customization, so different PointData and LineData keys can have distinct visual styles.


Replace global options with per-key option maps:
struct TemporalProjectionViewStateData {
    // ... existing fields ...

    // Replace flat point_size/line_width with per-key options:
    std::map<std::string, PointGlyphOptions> point_options;   // key → glyph options
    std::map<std::string, LineRenderOptions> line_options;     // key → line options
};
Keys not present in the map use default PointGlyphOptions / LineRenderOptions.



Replace the current flat spinboxes with a per-key options table, similar to LinePlotWidget’s per-series options table:

Point data table — add columns for glyph type, size, color
Line data table — add columns for color, width, alpha




In rebuildScene(), look up per-key options when building glyph styles and line colors:
for (auto const & pb : point_batches) {
    auto opts = lookupPointOptions(pb.key, _state->pointOptions());
    CorePlotting::GlyphStyle style;
    style.glyph_type = toRenderableGlyphType(opts.glyph_type);
    style.size = opts.glyph_size;
    style.color = hexToGlmVec4(opts.hex_color, opts.alpha);
    builder.addGlyphs("points_" + pb.key, pb.mapped, style);
}





Phase 3: Double-Click Time Navigation
    │
    │   (all independent of each other, can be done in any order)
    │
Phase 4: Polygon Selection
    └── uses: PolygonInteractionController (already implemented)
    └── needs: CorePlotting::Selection::selectPointsInPolygon (new)
    │
Phase 5: Selection → Group Integration
    ├── depends on: Phase 4 (polygon selection adds to selection set)
    │   (but can start with click/stroke selection only)
    └── depends on: Plots/Common/GroupManagementPanel
        (shared with LinePlotWidget, ScatterPlotWidget)
    │
Phase 6: Group-Based Coloring
    └── depends on: Phase 5 (group membership required)
    │
Phase 7: Subgroup Visibility Filtering
    └── depends on: Phase 5 (group membership required)
    │
Phase 8: Per-Key Rendering Options
    └── depends on: Phase 2 (glyph/line options defined)
Phases 1–3 are independent and can be implemented in any order. Phase 4 (polygon selection) is independent of 1–3 but provides the most natural multi-select workflow. Phase 5 (group integration) can begin with existing click/stroke selection but benefits from Phase 4. Phases 6 and 7 both depend on Phase 5 but are independent of each other. Phase 8 extends Phases 1 and 2 to per-key granularity.

Component
Status
Location
Used By

GlyphStyleControls widget

TemporalProjectionViewWidget, OnionSkinViewWidget, ScatterPlotWidget







Per-key vs. global rendering options: Phase 2 started with global options (simpler, now complete), extended to per-key options in Phase 8 to avoid premature complexity.
Polygon interaction: Uses the existing PolygonInteractionController from CorePlotting/Interaction/. This shared controller handles click-based polygon creation, vertex drag modification, cursor preview, and auto-close detection. Only a new selectPointsInPolygon() utility is needed for the ray-casting containment test.





Group color conflict resolution: When an entity belongs to multiple groups, which group’s color takes priority? Options: first group alphabetically, most recently assigned, or a blended color. First-match is simplest.
Visibility filtering performance: For very large datasets, should visibility filtering happen at the data-gathering stage (skip loading invisible entities entirely) or at the rendering stage (set visibility mask to 0)? The mask approach is simpler and sufficient for moderate dataset sizes.
MaskData support: The state struct has a comment noting “mask_data_keys deferred due to CPU contour extraction performance”. If GPU-based contour extraction becomes available, MaskData rendering could be added as a future phase.

title: Widget Development Guide
text: This guide walks through the systems that a new widget in WhiskerToolbox should integrate with. Each section describes what the system does, when you need it, and how to wire it up. The goal is not to duplicate the detailed reference docs — those are linked throughout — but to give you a map of the landscape and a concrete checklist.

title: Widget Development Guide
text:
Overview: What Makes a Widget
A WhiskerToolbox widget is a Qt6 QWidget that lives inside the Qt6AdvancedDocking dock system. Unlike a traditional Qt application where you manually create widgets and add them to layouts, WhiskerToolbox widgets are registered as types with the EditorRegistry, which manages their lifecycle, placement, and serialization.
A fully-featured widget integrates with up to six systems:








System
Purpose
Required?




EditorRegistry
Type registration, factory functions, dock placement
Yes — every widget


DataManager + Observer
Reading/writing shared data, reacting to changes
Yes — nearly every widget


Command Architecture
Serializable, undoable data mutations
When widget mutates DataManager


ParameterSchema + AutoParamWidget
Auto-generated config forms from C++ structs
When widget has configurable parameters


Context Actions
Right-click actions that open/configure your widget
When widget can be a target for data


Keymap System
Configurable keyboard shortcuts
When widget has keyboard-driven actions



The following diagram shows how these systems relate at runtime:
  User types a key                   User right-clicks data
        │                                    │
        ▼                                    ▼
 ┌──────────────┐                  ┌──────────────────┐
 │ KeymapManager│                  │ SelectionContext  │
 │ (event filter│                  │ (ContextActions)  │
 └──────┬───────┘                  └────────┬─────────┘
        │ dispatch                          │ execute()
        ▼                                   ▼
 ┌──────────────┐  ◄──── state ───  ┌──────────────┐
 │ KeyAction    │                   │ EditorRegistry│
 │ Adapter      │  ───── owns ───►  │ (type + state)│
 └──────┬───────┘                   └───────┬───────┘
        │                                   │ createEditor()
        ▼                                   ▼
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                   Your Widget                     │
 │                                                   │
 │  ┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────┐ │
 │  │ EditorState    │   │ AutoParamWidget         │ │
 │  │ (serializable) │   │ (generated from         │ │
 │  │                │   │  ParameterSchema)       │ │
 │  └────────┬───────┘   └────────────────────────┘ │
 │           │                                       │
 │           │ reads/writes via Commands              │
 │           ▼                                       │
 │     ┌──────────┐   notifyObservers()              │
 │     │DataManager├──────────────────────►callbacks  │
 │     └──────────┘                                  │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

text:
OperationContext — Inter-Widget Request/Response
When one widget needs structured data from another (e.g., a column config dialog requests a pipeline from the Transforms V2 editor), use OperationContext.
Detailed reference: Inter-Widget Communication Roadmap — Layer 3

As a Consumer (Requesting Data)
auto result = _operation_context->requestOperation(
    EditorLib::EditorInstanceId(_my_instance_id),
    EditorLib::EditorTypeId(QStringLiteral("TransformsV2Widget")),
    EditorLib::OperationRequestOptions{
        .channel = EditorLib::DataChannels::TransformPipeline,
        .keep_open_for_iteration = true
    });
Connect to operationDelivered and operationClosed signals to receive the response.


As a Producer (Providing Data)
Your widget checks for pending operations and shows a “Send to [requester]” button when one is active. When the user clicks it, call:
_operation_context->deliverResult(operation_id, result_payload);

title: Widget Development Guide
text:
Checklist: Creating a New Widget
Here is a step-by-step checklist for adding a new widget:

Minimum Viable Widget

Create MyWidgetState subclass of EditorState with reflect-cpp serializable data
Create MyWidget (the QWidget) and optionally MyWidgetProperties
Create MyWidgetRegistration.cpp with registerTypes() that registers EditorTypeInfo
Call registerTypes() from the application startup (where other widgets are registered)
Add CMakeLists.txt for the new widget and link required libraries



Data Integration

Accept std::shared_ptr<DataManager> in your factory/constructor
Register an observer callback to react to data changes
Store the CallbackID and remove the observer in the destructor
If the widget can be called from a background thread, use the QTimer::singleShot pattern



Optional: Command Integration

When the widget has “action buttons” that mutate DataManager, represent those as ICommands
Use commands::executeSequence() to dispatch
Consider undo support for destructive operations



Optional: Auto-Generated Parameter Forms

Define a reflect-cpp params struct for your algorithm/config
Optionally specialize ParameterUIHints<T> for tooltips and constraints
Create an AutoParamWidget from extractParameterSchema<T>()
Connect parametersChanged to your handler



Optional: Context Actions

Add a static void registerContextActions(EditorRegistry *, ...) helper in the anonymous namespace of your registration .cpp
Call it from registerTypes() before registry->registerType()
Implement is_applicable predicate based on data type/properties
Implement execute to open your widget and configure it with the selection
Use action IDs following <widget_domain>.<verb>_<noun> (e.g. my_widget.visualize_tensor)



Optional: Keyboard Shortcuts

Add a KeymapSystem::KeymapManager * parameter to registerTypes()
Add a static void registerEditorActions(KeymapSystem::KeymapManager *) helper in the anonymous namespace
Call it from registerTypes(), guarded by if (km)
Register KeyActionDescriptors with <widget_domain>.<verb>_<noun> action IDs
Create a KeyActionAdapter in the widget constructor with a handler lambda that dispatches by action_id
Remove the original keyPressEvent() / eventFilter() key handling once migrated



Optional: DataFocusAware

Inherit DataFocusAware and call connectToSelectionContext() if the widget should react to what the user has selected elsewhere



Optional: OperationContext

Implement consumer pattern if you need structured data from another widget
Implement producer pattern if other widgets should be able to request data from yours

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
text:
Keypoint labeling is a powerful method to systematically study motion, behavior, and anatomical positioning over time. By marking and tracking specific locations on subjects across frames in a video, you can extract detailed data about the dynamics of movement.
For example, keypoint data can be used to:
This tutorial will guide you through the process of labeling keypoints on a video and saving the keypoint data.

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
section: Step 1: Load Video or Existing Labels
text:
Step 1: Load Video or Existing Labels





To begin labeling:

Open the application and navigate to File > Load Data.
Select the video you intend to annotate.

Alternatively, if you’ve already created keypoints and want to review or update them:

Select File > Load JSON Configuration and choose your .json file.







Tip



See: Setting up a JSON File for more on configuration options.

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
text:
Step 2: Open the Data Manager





To create or manage point data:

Navigate to Modules > Data Manager to open the Data Manager Module.

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
section: Step 3: Create a New Keypoint Feature
text:
Step 3: Create a New Keypoint Feature





In the Data Manager:

Set the Output Directory: This is where your labeled data (CSV) will be saved.

Example: C:/Users/wanglab/Desktop/Cartoon_Mouse

Create New Data:

Type: point
Time Frame: Select based on your analysis requirements (e.g., time for temporal tracking).
Name: Choose a descriptive name (e.g., jaw, nose, or paw).


Click Create New Data to add the new feature.

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
section: Step 4: Edit and Add Keypoints in the Media Widget
text:
Step 4: Edit and Add Keypoints in the Media Widget





Once the point feature is created:

Enable the Feature: Select the feature in the media widget to activate the keypoint editor.
Customize Appearance:

Choose a color using the hex selector.
Adjust the opacity (Alpha) for better contrast against the video.
Modify the size and shape of the marker if needed.

Begin Labeling:

Switch mouse mode to “Select Point”.
Click anywhere in the video frame to add a point.
Clicking on an existing point will move it.













Important



Note: The keypoint is recorded as a single-pixel coordinate. Visual shape and style are only for display and are not saved.

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
section: Step 5: Review and Export Your Labels
text:
Step 5: Review and Export Your Labels





After labeling:

Select your feature (e.g., jaw) in the Data Manager.
You’ll see a spreadsheet with:

Frame indices
(x, y) coordinates for each labeled keypoint



Export Options:

File Name: Choose a meaningful name for your CSV.
Delimiter: (e.g., comma , or tab \t) – separates columns.
Line Ending: Select line break style (\n, \r\n, etc.).
Header: Optionally include a header row with custom labels.

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
text:
Optional: Export Matching Media Frames





You can export the video frames where keypoints were labeled:

Check Export Matching Media Frames.
Choose from export options:

Save by Frame Name
Frame ID Padding
Image Name Prefix
Subfolder for Images
Overwrite Existing Files








Warning



Keypoints will not be drawn on these frames. Only raw frames are exported.

title: Keypoint Video Labeling
text:
Step 6: Save to CSV





Once you’ve reviewed your labels:

Click “Save to CSV”

A confirmation will appear showing the file path.
Your labeled keypoint data is now saved and ready for further analysis.


Summary
This tutorial demonstrated how to:

Load a video or keypoint configuration
Create and configure keypoint data
Annotate frames with feature coordinates
Export label data and relevant frames



See Also

Point Transforms Reference

title: How to Import Video
text:
Overview
This guide shows you how to import video files into Neuralyzer for visualization and analysis. Videos are used as the primary media backdrop for viewing and annotating behavioral data such as whisker movements, facial expressions, or body tracking.






WarningVideo Encoding Requirements



Neuralyzer does not support videos encoded with B-frames. B-frames (bidirectional frames) use data from both past and future frames for compression, which breaks the simple sequential decoding strategy used for efficient random frame access.
If your video has B-frames, you must re-encode it before importing. See Checking for and Removing B-frames below.

title: How to Import Video
text:
Supported Video Formats
Neuralyzer uses FFmpeg for video decoding and supports common formats including:



Format
Extension
Notes




MPEG-4
.mp4
Recommended format


AVI
.avi
Older format, larger file sizes


QuickTime
.mov

title: How to Import Video
text:
Checking for and Removing B-frames
B-frames (bidirectional frames) use temporal compression that references both past and future frames. This breaks random access decoding strategies and will cause frame seeking issues in Neuralyzer.

Why B-frames Are Problematic
Most video players buffer ahead and can decode B-frames efficiently. However, for frame-by-frame analysis where you need instant random access to any frame, B-frame dependencies create significant overhead:

Seeking to frame N may require decoding frames before and after N
Frame-accurate positioning becomes unreliable
Scrubbing through video becomes slow or produces incorrect frames



Step 1: Check if Your Video Has B-frames
Use ffprobe (included with FFmpeg) to inspect the frame types:
ffprobe -show_frames my_video.mp4 | grep "pict_type" > frame_types.txt
This creates a file listing the type of each frame:

pict_type=I - Intra frame (keyframe, fully self-contained)
pict_type=P - Predicted frame (references previous frames only)
pict_type=B - Bidirectional frame (references past AND future frames) ⚠️

If you see any pict_type=B entries, you need to re-encode the video.






Tip



You can quickly check for B-frames with:
ffprobe -show_frames my_video.mp4 | grep "pict_type=B" | head
If this produces any output, B-frames are present.




Step 2: Re-encode to Remove B-frames
Use FFmpeg to create a B-frame-free version of your video:
ffmpeg -i my_video.mp4 -c:v h264_nvenc -profile:v baseline -bf:v 0 my_video_no_bframes.mp4
Command breakdown:







Flag
Description




-i my_video.mp4
Input video file


-c:v h264_nvenc
Use NVIDIA GPU encoder (fast). Use libx264 for CPU encoding


-profile:v baseline
H.264 baseline profile (no B-frames by definition)


-bf:v 0
Explicitly set B-frames to 0


my_video_no_bframes.mp4
Output file name









NoteCPU vs GPU Encoding




h264_nvenc - NVIDIA GPU encoder (very fast, requires NVIDIA GPU)
libx264 - CPU encoder (works everywhere, slower)

For CPU encoding, use:
ffmpeg -i my_video.mp4 -c:v libx264 -profile:v baseline -bf:v 0 my_video_no_bframes.mp4




Step 3: Verify the Re-encoded Video
Confirm the new video has no B-frames:
ffprobe -show_frames my_video_no_bframes.mp4 | grep "pict_type=B"
This should produce no output if the re-encoding was successful.

title: Introduction
text:
Neuralyzer (WhiskerToolbox) is an open-source desktop platform for neural and behavioral data analysis, developed by neuroscientists who use it every day. Its primary purpose is to act as both a reproducibility machine and a practical toolkit for data exploration.
In real experiments, it is hard to align all your data and visualize everything together. Doing this repeatedly across many concurrent data modalities can become complex and tedious. Neuralyzer is built as a workbench for behavioral and neural recordings so those multimodal workflows stay connected, time-aligned, and manageable.
Suppose you want to load a video of a mouse licking a spout and also load predicted tongue masks so you can track tongue area while optogenetic stimulation is being recorded.
In Neuralyzer, you can load all of these modalities, run transforms to compute mask area, derive intervals where licking occurs, and then measure how many licks fall inside each optogenetic stimulus event. Even when TTL events were recorded on a different acquisition path and may live in a different TimeFrame, the platform is designed to make this cross-modal analysis straightforward and easy to perform in one place.

title: Introduction
text:
What This Program Does

Core capabilities

Single-place data interaction: Keep signals, events, labels, media, and derived outputs in one connected workspace for exploration and decision-making.
Data ingestion and organization: Import analog signals, digital events/intervals, tensors, points, lines, masks, and media.
Unified analysis workflows: Apply transforms and feature extraction pipelines to convert raw data into interpretable outputs.
Interactive visualization: Explore data through time-series views, media overlays, event plots, scatter/heatmap views, and specialized widgets.
Machine learning support: Integrate supervised/unsupervised pipelines and dimensionality reduction for exploratory and predictive analysis.
Deep learning integration: Run encoder/post-encoder modules and use model-aware tooling for modern feature workflows.



Typical use cases

Curating and triaging long recordings.
Building reproducible processing pipelines for lab-specific modalities.
Comparing model outputs against raw signals and labels.
Exporting publication-ready summaries and plot-derived tables.

title: Introduction
text: How It Is Written

title: Introduction
text:
Architecture Overview

Application stack

Language and standard: C++23
GUI framework: Qt6
Build system: CMake presets
Testing: Catch2 (plus dedicated fuzz-test targets)

Speed is the primary reason the core platform is written in C++. The goal is to keep interaction responsive on large videos, high-rate neural streams, dense labels, and many concurrent modalities without sacrificing correctness or reproducibility.
The codebase is split into focused libraries, then composed into the main application. This separation keeps the UI responsive while protecting core logic from GUI coupling.


Library design
The platform is intentionally modular. Important layers include:

Data core: strongly typed temporal indexing and object storage/orchestration.
Processing layer: transforms, feature extraction, and conversion pipelines.
Visualization layer: plotting abstractions and backend renderers.
UI layer: editor-state driven widgets and dockable tools.

This arrangement allows teams to add data types or algorithms without destabilizing unrelated modules.


Extensibility model
WhiskerToolbox emphasizes registries and schemas:

Parameter schemas are extracted and used to auto-generate user-facing controls.
Processing and synthesis systems use registration patterns so new operations can be introduced cleanly.
IO and transform ecosystems are designed to accommodate both built-in and project-specific workflows.

title: Introduction
text:
General Philosophy

Read-first, write-intentionally
The baseline posture is conservative around data mutation: inspect first, validate assumptions, and write only when the user explicitly chooses to commit/export/save. This protects source datasets and keeps analysis sessions auditable.






ImportantNo-write-access mindset



The system is designed so that exploration and diagnosis can happen safely without forcing writes to canonical data. Persisting changes is an explicit step, not a side effect of simply viewing or analyzing data.




Scientific ergonomics over novelty
The interface and APIs prioritize:

clear provenance,
predictable transformations,
high signal-to-noise visual feedback,
and reproducibility under real lab constraints.



Speed-first with clarity
The implementation targets high throughput and low-latency interaction while preserving understandable abstractions. The goal is speed that remains maintainable by research and engineering teams over time.

title: Introduction
text:
Who This Is For
WhiskerToolbox is meant for people who need one environment to inspect heterogeneous data, connect manual review with algorithmic processing, and move from raw recordings to defensible results.
This includes:

Experimental neuroscientists working with synchronized video, electrophysiology, behavior labels, and stimulation events.
Behavioral scientists who need to annotate, curate, and quantify structure in long recordings.
Lab engineers and analysts building reproducible pipelines that can be rerun across cohorts and sessions.
Computational researchers who want to compare model outputs against raw data in the same interface.
Trainees and students who benefit from a visual, end-to-end workflow instead of stitching together many scripts and tools.

If your workflow spans media, labels, events, intervals, analog traces, and derived features, this platform is built for that intersection.

title: Creating Mask Labels
text: Creating mask labels is done through the GrabCut tool. Currently it can be opened through the Tongue Tracking widget.

title: Creating Mask Labels
text:
GrabCut Tool Operation

Selecting ROI
To start creating a mask, left click and drag the mouse over the image to form a green rectangle as the region of interest. The objected intended to be masked should be completely within this rectangle. If a mistake is made the reset button returns the tool to the initial state.
The GrabCut algorithm works as such: the algorithm keeps track of the mask and for each iteration, attempts to refine it. In between iterations, the user can tweak the mask to provide feedback to the algorithm, which will be noted through subsequent iterations.
After drawing an ROI the “Iterate Grabcut” button becomes functional. Using it completes one iteration of the GrabCut algorithm. The first usage of this button will show the initial mask created by the algorithm. Ideally the user should press this button throughout the editing process.

Opacity of the displayed mask can be adjusted with the transparency slider



User Feedback
In between iterations the user has access to a drawing bush whose radius can be adjusted. It is used to paint feedback for the GrabCut algorithm, which it will take into account upon pressing the “Iterate Grabcut” button. The brush has four colors:

“Definite Background”: Tells GrabCut the painted area is definitely not part of the mask.
“Definite Foreground”: Tells GrabCut the painted area is definitely part of the mask.
“Probable Background”: Suggests to GrabCut the painted area may not be part of the mask. GrabCut uses this information to create a better mask but may partially/fully disobey it.
“Probable Foreground”: Suggests to GrabCut the painted area is likely part of the mask. GrabCut uses this information to create a better mask but may partially/fully disobey it.



Saving and Exporting
The GrabCut tool may be exited at any time by pressing the “Exit” button. “Save and Exit” will exit the tool and save the mask into the main application and displayed in the media player. All created masks can be saved to disk using the “Save Drawn Masks” button in the Tongue Tracking widget.

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
This guide walks through fitting an Input-Output HMM (IOHMM) to classify whisker contact frames using deep-learning encoder features and the dynamax library (JAX-based).
A standard HMM models contact/no-contact as hidden states with a fixed transition matrix. At high frame rates this struggles because (1) the transition matrix is overwhelmingly self-transitioning, (2) the transition dynamics cannot adapt to the behavioral context — e.g., whether the animal is actively whisking or quiescent.
A standard GLM-HMM (Ashwood et al., 2022) improves emissions by making them input-dependent, but it still uses a fixed transition matrix. This means the probability of switching between behavioral regimes is constant regardless of what the animal is doing — which is the core limitation.
An Input-Output HMM solves this by making both transitions and emissions depend on the input features:
Input-driven transitions (IOHMM): \[
P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i,\; \mathbf{u}_t) =
\text{softmax}(\mathbf{V}_i \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{c}_i)_j
\]
Input-driven emissions (GLM): \[
P(y_t = \text{contact} \mid z_t = k,\; \mathbf{u}_t) =
\text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{b}_k)
\]
Each state \(k\) has its own transition weights \(\mathbf{V}_k\) and emission weights \(\mathbf{W}_k\), so both when the model transitions between states and how each state maps features to contact labels are learned from data.
Why input-dependent transitions matter: When the animal starts whisking vigorously, the input-dependent transition model can increase the probability of switching to a “contact-prone” state. When it stops whisking, transitions toward a “quiet” state become more likely. This context-sensitivity is impossible with a fixed transition matrix.
Why dynamax? The ssm library does not install on Python 3.12 (required for neuralyzer). dynamax is the JAX-based successor from the same group (probml). While dynamax provides CategoricalRegressionHMM (input-dependent emissions with fixed transitions), we build a custom IOHMM by subclassing its modular HMMTransitions component — following the custom HMM pattern.

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 0: Environment Setup
Create a dedicated conda environment with Python 3.12, then install the dependencies in the correct order. This step only needs to be done once.






Warning



Why the version pins? dynamax has no version constraints on its core dependencies (tensorflow_probability, jax, numpy are all unpinned). Running pip install dynamax pulls the latest of everything, but the latest releases are mutually incompatible:

JAX 0.5+ removes jax.interpreters.xla.pytype_aval_mappings (used by TFP).
NumPy 2.0+ renames np.reshape(newshape=...) to shape= (used by TFP).

The pins below are a known-working combination for dynamax.


# 1. Create the environment (Python 3.12 is required for neuralyzer)
conda create -n dynamax python=3.12 -y
conda activate dynamax

# 2. Install dynamax
pip install dynamax

# 3. Pin dependencies to a known-working combination
pip install jax==0.4.30 jaxlib==0.4.30 numpy==1.26.4 scipy==1.13.0 tensorflow-probability==0.24.0

# 4. Install IPython — required by fastprogress (a dynamax transitive dep)
#    for progress-bar display during EM fitting.
pip install ipython






Tip



GPU users: Replace step 3 with pip install "jax[cuda12]==0.4.30" jaxlib==0.4.30 ... to use an NVIDIA GPU.


Verify the environment is set up correctly:
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model import CategoricalRegressionHMM  # for reference
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.abstractions import HMM, HMMTransitions
import jax, numpy as np
print(f"JAX {jax.__version__}, NumPy {np.__version__}")  # 0.4.30, 1.26.4
print("Environment OK")

text:
Data Contract
Both training and prediction rely on three objects in a single DataManager session:








Key
Type
Description




features
TensorData (2D)
Shape \([T, D]\) — encoder features per frame


train
DigitalIntervalSeries
Training block intervals (in video time coordinates)


contact
DigitalIntervalSeries
Contact intervals (in video time coordinates)









Important



Time base mismatch: Intervals use TimeFrameIndex values (e.g., 37000) but the feature array is indexed by row (e.g., row 0). Each TensorData row has an associated TimeFrameIndex; we use findRowGreaterOrEqual() and findRowLessOrEqual() to convert interval boundaries to row indices. This follows the same pattern as the C++ MLCore classification pipeline.


Output: A new DigitalIntervalSeries written back to DataManager with predicted contact intervals from the GLM-HMM.

Pipeline
Encoder Features (TensorData)       Contact Labels (DigitalIntervalSeries)

        │  inputs u_t ∈ ℝ^D                       │  observations y_t ∈ {0,1}

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 1: Extract Data from DataManager
import numpy as np

# --- Encoder features: shape (T, D) ---
features_td = dm.getData("features")          # TensorData
X_all = np.array(features_td.values, copy=True)  # writable copy
T_total, D = X_all.shape
print(f"Feature matrix: {T_total} frames × {D} dimensions")
print(f"Row type: {features_td.rowType()}")  # should be 'TimeFrameIndex'

# --- Row ↔ TimeFrameIndex conversion helpers ---
# Each TensorData row has an associated TimeFrameIndex (a plain int in Python).
# We use the TensorData row-index API (same pattern as MLCore's ClassificationPipeline).
row_time_indices = features_td.rowTimeIndices()  # list of int, one per row
print(f"  Row 0 → TimeFrameIndex {int(row_time_indices[0])}")
print(f"  Row {T_total-1} → TimeFrameIndex {int(row_time_indices[-1])}")

def time_to_row(time_val):
    """Convert a TimeFrameIndex value to a feature-array row index (inclusive start)."""
    row = features_td.findRowGreaterOrEqual(int(time_val))
    return row if row is not None else T_total  # past end

def time_to_row_end(time_val):
    """Convert a TimeFrameIndex to the exclusive-end row index for an interval."""
    row = features_td.findRowLessOrEqual(int(time_val) - 1)
    return (row + 1) if row is not None else 0  # before start

def row_to_time(row_idx):
    """Convert a feature-array row index back to a TimeFrameIndex value."""
    return int(row_time_indices[row_idx])

# --- Training block intervals ---
train_intervals = dm.getData("train").toList()
print(f"Training blocks: {len(train_intervals)}")
for iv in train_intervals:
    r_s = time_to_row(iv.start)
    r_e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
    print(f"  TimeFrameIndex [{iv.start}, {iv.end}) → rows [{r_s}, {r_e})  ({r_e - r_s} frames)")

# --- Contact intervals ---
contact_intervals = dm.getData("contact").toList()
print(f"Contact intervals: {len(contact_intervals)}")

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
section: Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
text:
Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
We need a frame-level binary label \(y_t \in \{0, 1\}\) for each training block. dynamax expects a batch dimension: emissions shape is (num_batches, T, ...) and inputs shape is (num_batches, T, D).
import jax.numpy as jnp

def intervals_to_binary(total_frames, intervals):
    """Convert contact intervals to a binary array in feature-row space.

    Each interval's start/end is converted from TimeFrameIndex values to
    feature-array row indices using the TensorData row-index API.
    """
    labels = np.zeros(total_frames, dtype=np.int32)
    for iv in intervals:
        r_s = time_to_row(iv.start)
        r_e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
        labels[r_s:r_e] = 1
    return labels

# Build per-frame binary contact labels over the entire session (in row space)
y_all = intervals_to_binary(T_total, contact_intervals)
print(f"Total contact frames (row space): {y_all.sum()} / {T_total}")

# Standardise features (important for logistic regression convergence)
X_mean = X_all.mean(axis=0)
X_std = X_all.std(axis=0) + 1e-8
X_all_normed = (X_all - X_mean) / X_std

# Split into per-block arrays (converting TimeFrameIndex → row indices)
X_blocks = []  # list of (T_block, D) arrays — inputs
y_blocks = []  # list of (T_block,) arrays — integer class labels

for iv in train_intervals:
    s = time_to_row(iv.start)
    e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
    assert e > s, (
        f"Empty block after conversion: TimeFrameIndex [{iv.start},{iv.end}) → rows [{s},{e}). "
        f"Feature rows span TimeFrameIndex [{int(row_time_indices[0])}, {int(row_time_indices[-1])}]. "
        f"Check that the training interval overlaps the feature range."
    )
    X_blocks.append(X_all_normed[s:e])
    y_blocks.append(y_all[s:e])

print(f"Prepared {len(X_blocks)} training blocks")
for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(zip(X_blocks, y_blocks)):
    n_contact = int(yb.sum())
    pct = 100 * n_contact / len(yb) if len(yb) > 0 else 0.0
    print(f"  Block {i}: {len(yb)} frames, {n_contact} contact ({pct:.1f}%)")






Important



Padding for batched EM: dynamax’s fit_em requires all sequences in a batch to have the same length. If your training blocks differ in length, either:

Pad shorter blocks (shown below), or
Fit on each block separately with fit_sgd.

We show the padding approach here.


def pad_sequences(arrays, pad_value=0):
    """Pad a list of variable-length arrays to the same length along axis 0."""
    max_len = max(a.shape[0] for a in arrays)
    padded = []
    for a in arrays:
        pad_width = [(0, max_len - a.shape[0])] + [(0, 0)] * (a.ndim - 1)
        padded.append(np.pad(a, pad_width, constant_values=pad_value))
    return np.stack(padded)

# Pad and convert to JAX arrays
batch_emissions = jnp.array(pad_sequences(y_blocks, pad_value=0))   # (B, T_max)
batch_inputs = jnp.array(pad_sequences(X_blocks, pad_value=0.0))    # (B, T_max, D)

print(f"Batched emissions shape: {batch_emissions.shape}")
print(f"Batched inputs shape:    {batch_inputs.shape}")

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 3: Create the Input-Output HMM
dynamax does not include an IOHMM out of the box, but its modular architecture makes it straightforward to build one. We create a custom InputDrivenHMMTransitions class (following the custom HMM pattern) and combine it with the existing CategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions.






Note



How dynamax handles input-dependent transitions internally: The base HMMTransitions class already supports inputs in its API — the _compute_transition_matrices() method vmaps over time steps when inputs are provided, producing a (T-1, K, K) tensor of time-varying transition matrices. The gradient-based M-step also passes inputs through. We just need to implement distribution() so it actually uses the inputs.


import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax.random as jr
import optax
import tensorflow_probability.substrates.jax.distributions as tfd

from typing import NamedTuple, Optional, Tuple, Union
from jaxtyping import Float, Array

from dynamax.parameters import ParameterProperties
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.abstractions import (
    HMM, HMMTransitions, HMMParameterSet, HMMPropertySet
)
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.initial import (
    StandardHMMInitialState, ParamsStandardHMMInitialState
)
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.categorical_glm_hmm import (
    CategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions, ParamsCategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions
)
from dynamax.types import IntScalar, Scalar


# ── Input-Driven Transition Parameters ──────────────────────────────
class ParamsInputDrivenTransitions(NamedTuple):
    """Parameters for input-driven transitions.

    weights[i, j, :] are the feature weights for transitioning
    from state i to state j.
    """
    weights: Union[Float[Array, "num_states num_states input_dim"],
                   ParameterProperties]
    biases: Union[Float[Array, "num_states num_states"],
                  ParameterProperties]


# ── Input-Driven Transition Model ───────────────────────────────────
class InputDrivenHMMTransitions(HMMTransitions):
    r"""Transitions whose probabilities depend on external inputs.

    $$P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i, \mathbf{u}_t) =
      \text{softmax}(\mathbf{V}_i \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{c}_i)_j$$

    where $\mathbf{V}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times M}$ and
    $\mathbf{c}_i \in \mathbb{R}^K$.

    The base class `_compute_transition_matrices` and gradient-based
    `m_step` handle all the heavy lifting — we only implement
    `distribution`, `initialize`, and `log_prior`.
    """

    def __init__(self, num_states, input_dim,
                 m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
                 m_step_num_iters=50):
        super().__init__(m_step_optimizer=m_step_optimizer,
                         m_step_num_iters=m_step_num_iters)
        self.num_states = num_states
        self.input_dim = input_dim

    def distribution(self, params, state, inputs=None):
        logits = params.weights[state] @ inputs + params.biases[state]
        return tfd.Categorical(logits=logits)

    def initialize(self, key=None, method="prior",
                   transition_weights=None, transition_biases=None):
        if key is None:
            raise ValueError("key must be provided")

        key1, key2 = jr.split(key)

        if transition_weights is None:
            # Small random weights — features start with weak influence
            transition_weights = 0.01 * jr.normal(
                key1, (self.num_states, self.num_states, self.input_dim))

        if transition_biases is None:
            # Sticky initialisation: self-transitions are initially preferred
            transition_biases = 2.0 * jnp.eye(self.num_states)

        params = ParamsInputDrivenTransitions(
            weights=transition_weights, biases=transition_biases)
        props = ParamsInputDrivenTransitions(
            weights=ParameterProperties(),
            biases=ParameterProperties())
        return params, props

    def collect_suff_stats(self, params, posterior, inputs=None):
        # Override: pass full inputs to M-step. The base class slices
        # inputs[1:] here, but _compute_transition_matrices also slices
        # inputs[1:] internally — causing a double-slice shape mismatch.
        return posterior.trans_probs, inputs

    def log_prior(self, params):
        """Gaussian prior on weights (L2 regularisation)."""
        return -0.5 * jnp.sum(params.weights ** 2)


# ── Full IOHMM Parameter Set ───────────────────────────────────────
class ParamsIOHMM(NamedTuple):
    initial: ParamsStandardHMMInitialState
    transitions: ParamsInputDrivenTransitions
    emissions: ParamsCategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions


# ── Input-Output HMM ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class InputDrivenCategoricalRegressionHMM(HMM):
    r"""HMM with input-driven transitions AND input-driven emissions.

    **Transitions (IOHMM):**
    $$P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i, \mathbf{u}_t) =
      \text{softmax}(\mathbf{V}_i \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{c}_i)_j$$

    **Emissions (Categorical GLM):**
    $$P(y_t \mid z_t = k, \mathbf{u}_t) =
      \text{Cat}(\text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{b}_k))$$

    Unlike `CategoricalRegressionHMM`, the transitions are **not** a fixed
    matrix — they depend on the input features at each time step.
    """

    def __init__(self, num_states, num_classes, input_dim,
                 initial_probs_concentration=1.1,
                 transition_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
                 transition_m_step_num_iters=50,
                 emission_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
                 emission_m_step_num_iters=50):
        self.input_dim = input_dim

        initial_component = StandardHMMInitialState(
            num_states,
            initial_probs_concentration=initial_probs_concentration)

        transition_component = InputDrivenHMMTransitions(
            num_states, input_dim,
            m_step_optimizer=transition_m_step_optimizer,
            m_step_num_iters=transition_m_step_num_iters)

        emission_component = CategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions(
            num_states, num_classes, input_dim,
            m_step_optimizer=emission_m_step_optimizer,
            m_step_num_iters=emission_m_step_num_iters)

        super().__init__(num_states, initial_component,
                         transition_component, emission_component)

    @property
    def inputs_shape(self):
        return (self.input_dim,)

    def initialize(self, key=jr.PRNGKey(0), method="prior",
                   initial_probs=None,
                   transition_weights=None, transition_biases=None,
                   emission_weights=None, emission_biases=None):
        key1, key2, key3 = jr.split(key, 3)
        params, props = dict(), dict()

        params["initial"], props["initial"] = \
            self.initial_component.initialize(
                key1, method=method, initial_probs=initial_probs)
        params["transitions"], props["transitions"] = \
            self.transition_component.initialize(
                key2, method=method,
                transition_weights=transition_weights,
                transition_biases=transition_biases)
        params["emissions"], props["emissions"] = \
            self.emission_component.initialize(
                key=key3, method=method,
                emission_weights=emission_weights,
                emission_biases=emission_biases)

        return ParamsIOHMM(**params), ParamsIOHMM(**props)


num_states = 3     # K: number of hidden behavioral states
num_classes = 2    # binary outcome: contact / no-contact
input_dim = D      # encoder feature dimensionality

model = InputDrivenCategoricalRegressionHMM(
    num_states=num_states,
    num_classes=num_classes,
    input_dim=input_dim,
)

# Initialize parameters
params, props = model.initialize(key=jr.PRNGKey(0))
print(f"IOHMM: {num_states} states, {input_dim}-dim inputs, {num_classes} categories")
print(f"Transition weights shape: {params.transitions.weights.shape}")
print(f"Transition biases shape:  {params.transitions.biases.shape}")
print(f"Emission weights shape:   {params.emissions.weights.shape}")
print(f"Emission biases shape:    {params.emissions.biases.shape}")

Choosing the number of states

K=2 is the minimum: one state for “contact-responsive” frames and one for “non-responsive”.
K=3 is recommended: adds a transition/ambiguous state that absorbs boundary uncertainty.
Higher K may overfit; use cross-validation (see Cross-Validation) to select.



Tuning the M-step
The transition and emission components each use gradient descent for their M-step. You can tune the optimizer and number of iterations independently:
model_tuned = InputDrivenCategoricalRegressionHMM(
    num_states=num_states,
    num_classes=num_classes,
    input_dim=input_dim,
    transition_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-3),  # slower LR for transitions
    transition_m_step_num_iters=100,                # more iterations
    emission_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
    emission_m_step_num_iters=50,
)

section: Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
text:
Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
num_iters = 100

params, log_probs = model.fit_em(
    params,
    props,
    emissions=batch_emissions,
    inputs=batch_inputs,
    num_iters=num_iters,
)
print(f"Final log-probability: {log_probs[-1]:.2f}")

Multiple initialisations
EM finds a local optimum. Run several random initialisations and keep the best:
best_lp = -jnp.inf
best_params = None

for seed in range(5):
    cand_params, cand_props = model.initialize(key=jr.PRNGKey(seed))
    cand_params, lps = model.fit_em(
        cand_params, cand_props,
        emissions=batch_emissions,
        inputs=batch_inputs,
        num_iters=num_iters,
    )
    if lps[-1] > best_lp:
        best_lp = lps[-1]
        best_params = cand_params

params = best_params
print(f"Best log-probability across initialisations: {best_lp:.2f}")


Alternative: SGD fitting
If EM is slow or you want mini-batch training, use SGD instead:
import optax

params_sgd, losses = model.fit_sgd(
    params,
    props,
    emissions=batch_emissions,
    inputs=batch_inputs,
    optimizer=optax.adam(1e-3),
    num_epochs=100,
)


Print convergence
lps = np.array(log_probs)
print(f"Log-probability: {lps[0]:.2f} → {lps[-1]:.2f} over {len(lps)} iterations")
if len(lps) > 5 and abs(lps[-1] - lps[-5]) < 0.1:
    print("  ✓ Converged (last 5 iterations changed < 0.1)")
else:
    print("  ⚠ May not have converged — consider increasing num_iters")

text:
Step 5: Inspect the Fitted Model

Viterbi decoding (most likely state sequence)
Decode each training block using its unpadded data:
for i, (yb, xb) in enumerate(zip(y_blocks, X_blocks)):
    emissions_i = jnp.array(yb)      # (T_block,)
    inputs_i = jnp.array(xb)         # (T_block, D)
    states = model.most_likely_states(params, emissions_i, inputs=inputs_i)
    states_np = np.array(states)
    unique, counts = np.unique(states_np, return_counts=True)
    print(f"Block {i}: states = {dict(zip(unique, counts))}")


Inspect learned transition weights
Unlike a standard HMM, the IOHMM has no single transition matrix — transitions are recomputed at every time step from the features. To understand the learned dynamics, inspect the transition weight norms and biases:
trans_W = np.array(params.transitions.weights)   # (K, K, D)
trans_b = np.array(params.transitions.biases)     # (K, K)

print("Transition biases (act as baseline log-odds for each transition):")
print(np.around(trans_b, decimals=3))
print()
for i in range(num_states):
    for j in range(num_states):
        w = trans_W[i, j, :]
        print(f"  State {i+1}→{j+1}: ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}, "
              f"bias = {trans_b[i,j]:.3f}")


Evaluate mean transition matrix on training data
To get an intuitive summary, compute the average transition matrix over the training features:
def mean_transition_matrix(params, X_normed):
    """Average the input-dependent transition matrix over all frames."""
    W = np.array(params.transitions.weights)   # (K, K, D)
    b = np.array(params.transitions.biases)     # (K, K)
    logits = np.einsum("ijd,td->tij", W, X_normed) + b[None, :, :]  # (T, K, K)
    exp_logits = np.exp(logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    trans_mats = exp_logits / exp_logits.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return trans_mats.mean(axis=0)

avg_A = mean_transition_matrix(params, X_all_normed)
print("Mean transition matrix (averaged over all features):")
print(np.around(avg_A, decimals=3))


Inspect per-state GLM weights
weights = np.array(params.emissions.weights)   # (K, C, D)
biases = np.array(params.emissions.biases)     # (K, C)
for k in range(num_states):
    # For binary classification, the "contact" class weight is weights[k, 1, :]
    w = weights[k, 1, :] - weights[k, 0, :]   # contrast: contact vs no-contact
    print(f"State {k+1}: ||Δw|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}, "
          f"top-5 features = {np.argsort(np.abs(w))[-5:][::-1]}")
